Each run's span and wall time are taken from the first and last line of its own pre-dispatch ingress ledger, and durations are rounded to the second: 03:16:00 to 03:22:51, 6 min 51 s for the `http` row in `transport` mode; 03:23:44 to 03:30:38, 6 min 54 s for the `sdk` row; 04:08:32 to 04:15:23, 6 min 51 s for the `http` row in `transport+503` mode. No repetition was re-run; the `transport+503` sub-row is twenty new work items, not a re-run of the twenty the `transport` sub-row spent.
- Result (`experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a2-go-http/`, `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a2-go-http-503/` and `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a2-go-sdk/`, `summary.csv`, twenty rows each; every row in a run is identical to every other row in that run):
  - **`http` layer, `CLIENT_RETRIES=1 CLIENT_RETRY_ON=transport`** — 1 arrival in 20 of 20, so `messageId_reused`, `id_reused` and `body_identical` are `n-a` in 20 of 20. `injection_fired` 1, `executes` 0, `invocations` 0, and the client's single line reports `unexpected HTTP status: 503 Service Unavailable` in 20 of 20. Every one of the twenty response lines is `status: 0` with `injection: close-after-read`; the execution ledger and the mock's invocation ledger are empty for all twenty work items, which is the injection firing before the A2A SDK saw the request. The retry did not fire because in this mode it re-sends on a transport error and never on a response, and the waypoint gave the client a response.
  - **`http` layer, `CLIENT_RETRIES=1 CLIENT_RETRY_ON=transport+503`** — 2 arrivals in 20 of 20; `messageId_reused` **yes** in 20 of 20, `id_reused` **yes** in 20 of 20, `body_identical` **yes** in 20 of 20. Across all twenty work items the two arrivals carry 1 distinct `messageId`, 1 distinct JSON-RPC `id`, 1 distinct `body_sha256` and 1 distinct `body_len`: the second delivery is the first one's bytes, unchanged. All forty arrivals carry `a2a_version` `1.0` and came from `10.244.1.55`. `injection_fired` 1, `executes` 1, `invocations` 1 in 20 of 20; the response lines are twenty `status: 0` with `injection: close-after-read` and twenty `200`; the execution ledger holds `received=1, execute=1, state=3, result=1` per work item and the mock recorded one call per work item, `caller worker`, `outcome ok`, `injection none`. The client printed **one** line, `attempt 1`, `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, with no error: an HTTP-layer retry is invisible above the transport, so the caller never learns there were two deliveries.
  - **`sdk` layer, `CLIENT_SDK_RESEND=on`** — 2 arrivals in 20 of 20; `messageId_reused` **yes** in 20 of 20, `id_reused` **no** in 20 of 20, `body_identical` **no** in 20 of 20. Across all twenty work items the two arrivals carry 1 distinct `messageId`, 2 distinct JSON-RPC `id`s, 2 distinct `body_sha256`, and **1 distinct `body_len`** — the two bodies are the same length and differ only in the id field, both ids being UUIDs. All forty arrivals carry `a2a_version` `1.0`. `injection_fired` 1, `executes` 1, `invocations` 1 in 20 of 20; the response lines are twenty `status: 0` with `injection: close-after-read` and twenty `200` with no injection; the execution ledger holds `received=1, execute=1, state=3, result=1` per work item, so the receiver created one Task, and the mock recorded one call per work item, `caller worker`, `outcome ok`, `injection none`. The two client lines per repetition are `attempt 1` with `unexpected HTTP status: 503 Service Unavailable` and `attempt 2` with `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`.
- Interpretation: for a2a-go v2.5.0, the answer to the box's three questions depends on which layer retries, and this run measured both. **At the SDK layer the messageId is reused and the JSON-RPC id is not**, in 20 of 20: `a2a.SendMessageRequest` carries the `Message` the caller built, including its `ID`, and `SendMessage` does not touch it, while `jsonrpcTransport.newHTTPRequest` mints `ID: uuid.NewString()` on every call, so handing the same request object back to the client produces a second delivery that a receiver keying on `messageId` would recognise as the same message and a receiver keying on the JSON-RPC id would not. The body therefore differs, but only in that one field: same length, same everything else — which is exactly the A.1 M2 stimulus, and A.1 already counted what this receiver does with it, namely create a second Task and call the model again. That did not happen here only because the first attempt never reached the executor: the injection refused it before dispatch, so the second delivery was the first one the receiver actually worked on, and the counts are one Task and one model call rather than two. **At the HTTP layer everything depends on what the retry is told to re-send on, and both answers were counted.** On a transport-error policy nothing was re-sent, 20 of 20, and the reason is the path rather than the client: the probe shows the waypoint converting the worker's mid-request connection close into a 503 before the client can see it, and a transport-error policy is by definition blind to a response. On a 503 policy the same client re-sent every time, 20 of 20, and **what it put on the wire was the first delivery's bytes exactly**: the same `messageId`, the same JSON-RPC id, the same body hash, the same length. That is the sharpest contrast in this entry. The two layers produce two different second deliveries from the same client: the HTTP layer an exact duplicate, indistinguishable from a transport replay, which is A.1's M1 stimulus; the SDK layer a new RPC carrying the old message, which is A.1's M2. A receiver's only handle on either is the `messageId`, which both preserve. The consequence for A.3 is narrower than it first looked and more useful: an HTTP-layer client retry behind this waypoint is not impossible, it is conditional on the policy being written against a response class, because the connection-level failure the receiver actually produced never reaches the client as one. A matrix row that configures R1 as a transport-error retry will count zero duplicates and record a false negative; configured against 503 it produces exactly one exact duplicate per failure, and the ledger can tell it apart from an SDK-level resend by the JSON-RPC id alone. Nothing here contradicts the specification, which says in §3.3.1 that Send Message operations **MAY** be idempotent and that agents *may* use `messageId` to detect duplicates: a client that keeps the `messageId` across a retry is giving a receiver the means to deduplicate, and this SDK does keep it.
- Follow-up: none. Neither behaviour is a project gap: a2a-go reusing the caller's `messageId` and minting a fresh JSON-RPC id per call is what its own code does and is consistent with the specification, and a proxy answering 503 when an upstream connection goes away mid-request is ordinary proxy behaviour rather than a defect, so there is nothing to report upstream. It is recorded here because it changes which layer can produce a duplicate delivery on this path.

Across all twenty work items the two arrivals carry 1 distinct `messageId`, 2 distinct JSON-RPC `id`s, 2 distinct `body_sha256` and **1 distinct `body_len`** — same length, differing only in the id field, both ids being UUIDs. All forty arrivals carry `a2a_version` `1.0`. `injection_fired` 1, worker `executes` 1, `invocations` 1 in 20 of 20; the worker's response lines are twenty `status: 0` with `injection: close-after-read` and twenty `200`, its execution ledger holds `received=1, execute=1, state=3, result=1` per work item, and the mock recorded one call per work item, `caller worker`, `outcome ok`, `injection none`. - Interpretation: for a2a-python 1.1.2 the answer matches a2a-go v2.5.0 exactly, which is the more useful half of this result. **At the SDK layer the messageId is reused and the JSON-RPC id is not**, in 20 of 20, with the body differing only in that field: `Forwarder` sets `Message.message_id` once, `BaseClient.send_message` calls `_apply_client_config`, which touches only `request.configuration` and under this configuration touches nothing at all, and `JsonRpcTransport.send_message` builds a fresh `JSONRPC20Request(..., _id=str(uuid4()))` on every invocation. So handing the same request object back to the client produces a second delivery a receiver keying on `messageId` would recognise as the same message and a receiver keying on the JSON-RPC id would not — the same shape the Go client produced, from independent code, and the same shape as A.1's M2 stimulus. As in the Go entry, the counts are one Task and one model call rather than two only because the injection refused the first attempt before dispatch. **At the HTTP layer the three sub-rows separate three different things, and only the third re-sent anything.** httpx's `retries` is not a request retry at all: httpcore applies it inside `_connect`, catching `ConnectError` and `ConnectTimeout`, so a request already written and then failed is outside its scope whatever the failure looked like — and this one had been written, since the worker read the body before closing. `ResendOnceTransport` in its default mode covers exactly that gap but only for an `httpx.TransportError`, and the waypoint had already turned the connection close into a 503, which reaches httpx as `HTTPStatusError`. Given a policy written against that response class, the same transport re-sent on every repetition and **put the first delivery's bytes back on the wire unchanged**: the same `messageId`, the same JSON-RPC id, the same body hash, the same length, 20 of 20 — the identical result the Go client's HTTP layer produced, again from independent code. So both clients now agree at both layers: the HTTP layer produces an exact duplicate, which is A.1's M1 stimulus, and the SDK layer a new RPC carrying the old message, which is A.1's M2. The consequence for A.3 is the one the Go entry drew: an HTTP-layer client retry behind this waypoint is conditional on the policy naming a response class rather than a transport error, and a matrix row configured the other way will count zero duplicates and record a false negative. The Python-specific warning is sharper still, because `httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(retries=n)` is the obvious thing to reach for and is not a request retry at any mode: it cannot be widened, it has no equivalent of the 503 case, and anyone setting it expecting request retries would measure a duplicate rate of zero and conclude something false about their client. Nothing here contradicts the specification, which in §3.3.1 makes Send Message idempotency a **MAY** and `messageId`-based duplicate detection optional: both clients keep the `messageId` across a retry, which is what gives a receiver the option.
- Follow-up: none. The SDK's identity behaviour, httpx's connection-scoped `retries` and the transport resend's own modes all match their source, read at the pinned versions, and a proxy answering 503 when an upstream connection goes away mid-request is ordinary proxy behaviour rather than a defect, so there is nothing to report upstream.

The lab's own additions and their defaults are read from the code and from the tests that fail if a default changes, listed in the table below and in `sources.md`.

  | Client | Layer | At the pinned version |
  |---|---|---|
  | a2a-go v2.5.0 | SDK option | **none.** `Config` has four fields (`PushConfig`, `AcceptedOutputModes`, `PreferredTransports`, `DisableTenantPropagation`) and the seven `FactoryOption`s are `WithConfig`, `WithTransport`, `WithCompatTransport`, `WithCallInterceptors`, `WithDefaultsDisabled`, `WithJSONRPCTransport` and `WithRESTTransport`.   | a2a-go v2.5.0 | lab addition, SDK re-invocation | **added for A.2, default off.** `CLIENT_SDK_RESEND=on` hands the same request object to `client.SendMessage` once more. |
  | a2a-python 1.1.2 | SDK option | **none.** `ClientConfig`'s eight fields are `streaming`, `polling`, `httpx_client`, `grpc_channel_factory`, `supported_protocol_bindings`, `use_client_preference`, `accepted_output_modes`, `push_notification_config`. The package does not contain the word. |

  | a2a-python 1.1.2 | lab addition, SDK re-invocation | **added for A.2, default off.** `CLIENT_SDK_RESEND=on` hands the same `SendMessageRequest` object to `client.send_message` once more. |

  Every lab knob is asserted off by a test that fails if its default changes: `TestNew_DefaultsHaveNoRetries` and `TestKnobs_DefaultOff` for the Go pair, `test_knobs_default_off` and `test_transport_retries_setting_recorded` for the Python three, plus `TestKnobs_UnreadableValuesLeaveTheKnobOff` for the rule that a value which is not a positive integer, or not exactly `on`, leaves a knob off rather than being guessed at. In their default mode the two HTTP-layer additions are asserted never to re-send after a response by `TestNewRetrying_DoesNotRetryOnResponse`, `TestNewRetrying_DoesNotRetryOn503ByDefault` and `test_resend_once_transport_does_not_resend_a_response`; in the 503 mode they are asserted to re-send after a 503 and after no other status by `TestNewRetrying_503ModeDoesNotRetryOnOtherResponses` and `test_resend_once_transport_on_503_does_not_resend_other_statuses`, and the mode itself is asserted to need its exact name, and not to be a switch of its own, by `TestParseRetryOn_DefaultsToTransport`, `TestKnobs_RetryOnModeIsAskedForByName` and `test_retry_on_mode_is_asked_for_by_name`. For completeness, the lab's one remaining retry-capable layer is not an A2A client: the model client's `MODEL_MAX_RETRIES`, default `0` against the `openai` package's own default of 2, which is the A.3 matrix's R3 row and not A.2's subject.
- Interpretation: as documented, and the same answer from both SDKs — **neither offers a retry, and both hand the question to the HTTP client the caller supplies.** That is not an omission the two projects share by accident: three doc comments in a2a-go say so explicitly, and a2a-python says nothing at all because its transport simply sends through whatever `httpx.AsyncClient` it was given. The practical consequence for this lab is the one the two A.2 entries above measured: because no retry exists to be switched on, every retry in Experiment A is one the lab added on purpose, at a named layer, off by default and switched on for one measured row, so a second delivery counted at a receiver is always attributable to a layer rather than to an SDK default nobody chose. It also sets the boundary of what the caller's HTTP client can do for them. On the Go side the caller's client is a full retry seat, and the lab uses it. On the Python side the seat looks equivalent but is not: `retries` covers connection attempts and nothing after the request was written, which is why the A.2 Python HTTP-layer row had to be measured three times, and why the first two produced no second delivery. Anyone reading the httpx keyword as a general request retry would be measuring something other than what they think. **And the layer is only half the answer: behind this gateway an HTTP-layer retry has to be written against a response class, not against a transport error, because a receiver-side connection close reaches the client as a 503** — which is what the lab's `CLIENT_RETRY_ON` mode names, `transport` against `transport+503`, and what the two A.2 entries above counted on each side of.
- Follow-up: none. No project gap here to reproduce: both SDKs delegate deliberately and say so, and httpx's `retries` is documented in its own module docstring as connection retries, so nothing is behaving other than as its source states.

- Result: spans accepted by the collector **1** (`POST /v1/traces` -> HTTP 200, body `{"partialSuccess":{}}`; that response line is captured in `probe-post.txt`, which repeats the same request under a separate work item for the capture and is evidence only, not a second count); spans the collector exported **1** (its `debug` exporter logged `"resource spans": 1, "spans": 1`, `collector-debug.txt`); spans returned by the trace backend for `lab.work_item=pipeline-probe-065020` **1**; rows in `spans.csv` **1**, with `lab_work_item=pipeline-probe-065020`, `service=pipeline-probe`, `duration_us=12000` and `http_status=200`, so the `transform` processor ran. All four identity attributes were lifted, not only the queried one: the raw response carries `lab.work_item`, `lab.message_id`, `lab.task_id` and `lab.caller` alongside the four `http.request.header.*` attributes they were read from. Prometheus targets **8 up of 8**: `istiod` 1 (`:15014/metrics`), `ztunnel` 2 (both nodes, `:15020/metrics`), `agentgateway-proxies` 4 (`:15020/metrics` on the two istiod-driven waypoints in `lab`, the ingress in `agentgateway-system` and the egress in `agentgateway-egress`), `otel-collector` 1 (`:8889/metrics`); no target had a `lastError`. A query for a work item that was never sent returns 0 rows and exit status 2, so "no trace" is distinguishable from "query failed" (`export-trace-negative.txt`). Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-pipeline/` (`pipeline-probe-065020/trace.json`, `pipeline-probe-065020/spans.csv`, `probe-span.json`, `probe-post.txt`, `export-trace-negative.txt`, `prometheus-targets.txt`, `collector-debug.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `replicasets.txt`, `sources.md`); the same response is committed as `experiments/fixtures/jaeger-trace-sample.json` and `make test` re-derives `experiments/fixtures/jaeger-trace-sample.spans.csv` from it.
- Interpretation: as documented, on every point that was checkable against a document, and with one measured surprise that is about this repository rather than about the pipeline. The documented pieces held: the trace backend's image binds every listener without configuration because its Dockerfile sets `JAEGER_LISTEN_HOST=0.0.0.0`, so the all-in-one default with in-memory storage needed no ConfigMap; its `/api/v3/traces` binding accepted `query.attributes` as a URL-encoded JSON map matched against span attributes and answered inside the documented `{"result": ...}` envelope with identifiers as lowercase hex; the collector's OTTL indexed the list-valued header attribute with `[0]` as its language reference says a `pcommon.Slice` can be; and the four scrape ports read out of the Istio charts, ztunnel's source and agentgateway's data-plane page were all answering. The surprise is that `make step-3` rotated all three `lab` pods, which the step-2c comment's claim about repeat applies had not led me to expect. `replicasets.txt` records why, and the two halves have different causes. **The worker and the mock rolled because `ko` rebuilt them from unchanged sources to different digests**: the worker went from revision 15 to 16 and the mock from 8 to 9, and the same file shows the worker carrying a different digest at every one of revisions 10 through 16, so a new digest per apply is the rule here rather than this occasion. **The orchestrator rolled for an unrelated reason, and my first reading of it was wrong.** I inferred from creation timestamps that the live template had carried two Gate 2 retry knobs; revision numbers say otherwise, and they are what decides which template is live. A ReplicaSet is reused and renumbered when a Deployment returns to a template it has held before, so the newest revision can sit on an older object: revision 45, knob-free, was created at 04:06:12Z and made current again afterwards (its `revision-history` annotation reads `41,43`), superseding revision 44, which carried `CLIENT_TRANSPORT_RESEND` and `CLIENT_RETRY_ON` and was created a minute later at 04:07:19Z. So the live template immediately before step 3 was revision 45 and **no retry knob was set on the object before the apply or after it**. Revision 46 differs from 45 in one respect only: the declared manifest lists `DOWNSTREAM_A2A_URL` fifth where `kubectl set env` and the A.2 restore had left it ninth, same nine names, same nine values. That ordering difference is a pod-template change, so the Deployment rolled. The lesson that survives is only the operational one: step 3 is a setup target like the others and must not be run against a measurement in progress, which is now written where the target is defined. Nothing here says anything yet about whether an agent's spans reach this pipeline: no pod is annotated for injection and no Go binary is wrapped, which is Task 1.
- Follow-up: none. No document was contradicted by what was observed. One inconsistency inside the OpenTelemetry Operator repository at tag v0.158.0 is recorded in `versions.yaml` rather than filed: its release notes, `versions.txt` and the default in `internal/config/config.go` all name Python auto-instrumentation `0.64b0`, while `autoinstrumentation/python/requirements.txt` at the same tag pins the `0.65b0` packages. The pin follows the three that agree, and the image that ran is the one this lab named.
- Note (2026-09-10): the Method above describes `make step-3` as that target stood on 2026-09-09. Since branch `followups-1` it installs no OpenTelemetry Operator — the Helm step was removed from the repository and the release, its four CRDs and its namespace were removed from the cluster on 2026-09-10 by the author's decision — so the Method no longer reproduces verbatim. **The counts above stand**: the probe span, the scrape targets and the pipeline they travelled never went through the Operator, and re-running this entry needs only the Helm step dropped from the command. `## Gate 3 / both receivers / trace per work item after the Operator removal` re-counts the trace shape on the cluster without it.

## Gate 3 / both receivers / trace per work item — Does one trace follow a work item across every hop, and which hops are missing?
- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.2 openai-python=3.9.0
- Environment: kind
- Method: `experiments/gate3-trace-per-work-item.sh` with `REPS=5`, once per receiver: one clean SendMessage per repetition, ten work items in all, nothing injected and no retry knob set. Telemetry pins: collector=otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.160.0, jaeger=jaegertracing/jaeger:2.20.0, prometheus=prom/prometheus:v3.14.0, operator=v0.158.0 (Helm chart 0.122.0), otel-go=v1.46.0, otel-go-contrib=v0.71.0, and for the Python agent the OpenTelemetry distro 0.65b0 with exporter 1.44.0 and the Starlette and httpx instrumentations at 0.65b0. The certificate check ran first and found `VALID CERT true` for `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/lab/sa/default` (`certificates.txt`), so ztunnel was not restarted. Paths as in Gate 2: the worker is reached in-cluster through its own istiod-driven agentgateway waypoint; the orchestrator's card is fetched in-cluster through the orchestrator's waypoint and its SendMessage POST enters through the agentgateway ingress, after which the orchestrator forwards to the worker through the worker's waypoint and the worker calls the model through the egress waypoint. What is instrumented: the three Go binaries by `internal/otel` (an `otelhttp` handler wrapper that copies the four identity headers onto the server span as `lab.*`, and an `otelhttp` transport wrapper); the Python agent by the OpenTelemetry distro installed in its own image and started by `opentelemetry-instrument` in its Procfile, configured only by environment, capturing the four identity headers on both its server and its client spans (`launcher-proof.txt` shows the pod has no injection init container, no injection annotation, and a process whose launcher-set `PYTHONPATH` points inside the image's own virtualenv); and the ingress and egress proxies by one `AgentgatewayPolicy` each. Because an A2A request carries the work item only inside `Message.metadata`, every lab client also sends the identity headers: the load client sends `X-Logical-Work-Item-Id` and `X-Caller` on every request of its Job, and the orchestrator's forwarder sends those two plus `X-A2A-Message-Id`. After each work item, `make ledgers` and `make export-trace`; the export runs inside the run because the trace backend stores in memory. Three further measurements outside the repetitions: the spike (one `AgentgatewayPolicy` of the same shape targeting the istiod-driven waypoint `agentgateway-waypoint`, one clean request, then the proxy's own `/config_dump`), the import resolution inside the running Python pod under both `PYTHONPATH` orderings the OpenTelemetry Operator can produce (`injection-shadowing.txt`), and four single-request states of the Operator's injection route, which the author decided on 2026-09-09 not to keep.
- Result: **the ledgers are identical in 5 of 5 per receiver**, with per-work-item counts scoped to each agent's own ledgers and model invocations counted for the work item as a whole, the way the `## Gate 2 / instruments / single clean request` entry scopes them. Worker receiver: 1 delivery, 1 executor entry, 1 Task at the worker, and nothing at the orchestrator, which is not on that path; 1 model invocation; client `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`. Orchestrator receiver: 1 delivery, 1 executor entry and 1 Task at the orchestrator, **and the same three again at the worker it forwards to**, so a collection for one of these work items holds 2 arrivals, 2 executor entries and 2 Tasks in all; 1 model invocation, which is the worker's; client `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`. **The span shape is identical in 5 of 5 per receiver.** Worker receiver: **8 spans** across **2 trace ids** (2 spans and 6), by service `loadgen`=2, `worker`=3, `agw-egress`=2, `mockllm`=1; `lab.work_item` on **3 of 8**. Orchestrator receiver: **62 spans** across **2 trace ids** (4 and 58), by service `loadgen`=2, `agentgateway-ingress`=2, `orchestrator`=53, `worker`=2, `agw-egress`=2, `mockllm`=1; `lab.work_item` on **5 of 62** (the orchestrator's card-fetch and SendMessage server spans, its client span for the forward, the worker's SendMessage server span, and the mock's). Of the orchestrator's 53 spans, 45 come from the A2A Python SDK's own tracer and 5 from the ASGI instrumentation's send and receive events. The two trace ids per work item are the card fetch and the message; each has a `loadgen` span as its root. **Hops that produced no span: the istiod-driven agentgateway waypoints, and only those** — `agentgateway-waypoint` for the worker receiver, both it and `agentgateway-waypoint-orch` for the orchestrator receiver. They are on the path and are handling the trace context: each work item has exactly **2 spans whose parent span id names no exported span** (worker receiver: the worker's card-fetch and SendMessage server spans; orchestrator receiver: the orchestrator's card-fetch server span and the worker's SendMessage server span), so each waypoint read the incoming `traceparent`, made a span id of its own, passed it on, and exported nothing. **The spike answers why, and it is not a configuration this lab got wrong**: the policy targeting `agentgateway-waypoint` was accepted by agentgateway's controller (`Accepted` True `Valid`, `Attached` True "Attached to all targets", `controllerName: agentgateway.dev/agentgateway`), and the proxy that istiod programs holds **0 policies** and `"tracing": null` in its own `/config_dump`, and emitted **0 spans** (`spike.txt`). The policy was removed again and is not in the overlay. **The Operator's injection route was measured in four states and is not the one the lab runs** (`python-injection/`, one request each, counts from the same three ledgers): with the Operator's default `PYTHONPATH`, its `protobuf` 7.36.0 shadows the agent's 6.33.6, which `a2a-sdk` 1.1.2 requires (`protobuf<7,>=5.29.5`), and the request counted **1 delivery, 0 executor entries, 0 Tasks, 0 model invocations** with `'FieldDescriptor' object has no attribute 'label'` on the execution and client ledgers; with the agent's `site-packages` named in the container's `PYTHONPATH` and image `0.64b0`, whose `opentelemetry-api` 1.43.0 is shadowed by the agent's 1.44.0 inside the shared `opentelemetry` namespace package, the request counted a healthy **1/1/1/1** with **0 orchestrator spans**, auto-initialisation having died with `ImportError: cannot import name '_OTEL_PYTHON_EVENT_LOGGER_PROVIDER'`; and two states worked identically, image `0.65b0` with that `PYTHONPATH` entry, and image `0.64b0` with `opentelemetry-api` pinned to 1.43.0 in the agent's own lockfile, each **1/1/1/1** with **64 spans**. `injection-shadowing.txt` is the import resolution behind all four, read by running the agent's own interpreter in the running pod: under the Operator's default it imports `protobuf` 7.36.0 from the injected directory, under the reordered path its own 6.33.6, and the `opentelemetry` namespace package spans both directories either way. One background number, for the rows that come next: with no work item in flight, the collector's own `otelcol_receiver_accepted_spans` counter rose by **150 in 60 seconds**, all of it on the OTLP HTTP receiver and none on the gRPC one the two gateway proxies use (`collector-idle-rate.txt`, two reads of the collector's metrics endpoint a minute apart). The three lab pods' readiness probes are the only traffic in that window, and the arithmetic of the probe periods accounts for the number exactly: 30 probes a minute each, one span per probe at the worker and the mock and three at the orchestrator. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-trace-per-work-item/` (`summary.csv`, one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json` and `spans.csv`, plus `span-detail.txt`, `spike.txt`, `launcher-proof.txt`, `injection-shadowing.txt`, `collector-idle-rate.txt`, `python-injection/`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`).
- Interpretation: one trace does follow a work item through every hop that exports at all, and the identity headers make it findable, but a work item is two traces rather than one and only three of the seven hop kinds carry `lab.work_item` on a span of their own. The split is the client's, not the mesh's: the load client fetches the agent card and sends the message as two separate root spans, and nothing joins them, so a query by work item returns two traces. Within the message trace the spans name each other as parents across every hop except the waypoint hops: loadgen to ingress to orchestrator holds, and worker to egress to mock holds, while the one link between them, the orchestrator's forward to the worker, is broken because the waypoint that carried it exported nothing. The attribute is present exactly where a lab component put a header on the wire and something read it back, and absent on the load client's own spans, on the gateways' spans, and on the spans the A2A Python SDK emits from its own tracer. That is enough for the matrix: `export-trace` queries by the attribute and the backend returns whole traces, so one matching span pulls in every hop of that trace. The one hop kind that is genuinely dark is the istiod-driven waypoint, and the two control planes disagree about it rather than either being silent: Istio documents that its own APIs, the Telemetry API included, are not applied to agentgateway proxies and names no replacement, so having no route to tracing there is not contradicted by any document read here; what is new is that agentgateway's controller accepts a policy for such a Gateway and reports it attached to a proxy it does not program. For A.3 this means a second delivery that crosses a waypoint will have to be attributed from the receiver's span and the ledgers rather than from a proxy span, and the dangling parent is itself the evidence that a waypoint sat between two exported spans. The Python instrumentation is the sharper finding of the day, and it is why the lab does not use the Operator's injection: zero-code instrumentation that ships a full dependency set and puts it ahead of the application's is not zero-code when the two overlap, and both directions of that overlap broke this agent, one by stopping it serving and one by stopping it exporting. The distro installed in the agent's own image and started by a launcher produces the same shape from a lockfile that resolves once and stays consistent with itself: 62 spans where the two working injection states produced 64, the gap being the downstream agent-card fetch, which a Python process makes once in its life and which those three single-request states each paid for as the first request after a rollout.
- Follow-up: `docs/upstream/otel-operator-python-injection-shadows-app-dependencies.md` (draft, not filed) for the two shadowing failures, which are the instrumentation breaking the application it instruments; `docs/upstream/agentgateway-policy-attached-to-istiod-driven-waypoint.md` (draft, not filed) for the status that says a policy is attached to a proxy its controller does not configure. The spike's own outcome, that an istiod-driven waypoint has no route to tracing, is recorded as not documented rather than as a contradiction, and is not filed.

## Gate 3 / n/a / gateway retry mechanics — Does the HTTPRoute retry fire on a POST and replay the same body, on each of the three routes?
- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.2 openai-python=3.9.0
- Environment: kind
- Method: `experiments/gate3-gateway-retry-mechanics.sh` three times on 2026-09-09, `ROUTE=waypoint`, `ROUTE=ingress` and `ROUTE=egress`, five repetitions each, fifteen work items in all, each invocation preceded by its own one-repetition dry run whose directory was deleted and whose id, like every other, carries the run's wall-clock nonce and is never reused. Telemetry pins: collector=otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.160.0, jaeger=jaegertracing/jaeger:2.20.0, prometheus=prom/prometheus:v3.14.0, operator=v0.158.0 (Helm chart 0.122.0), otel-go=v1.46.0, otel-go-contrib=v0.71.0, and for the Python agent the OpenTelemetry distro 0.65b0. The certificate check ran first on each invocation and found `VALID CERT true` for `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/lab/sa/default` (`certificates.txt`), so ztunnel was not restarted. Every invocation asserted `kubectl get httproute -A -o yaml | grep -c 'retry:'` = 0 before it began and left it at 0 afterwards (`control.txt`). **The stanza under test** is `retry: {attempts: 1, backoff: 100ms, codes: [503]}`, and `codes: [500, 503]` on the egress route because the failure injected on that hop is the model endpoint's `http500`; 500 and 503 are both inside the set Gateway API v1.6.2 says every implementation must support as retriable. The field is `<gateway:experimental>` at that version and is present only in the experimental CRD this lab installs, which the cluster confirms rather than the install URL: the installed `httproutes.gateway.networking.k8s.io` carries `bundle-version: v1.6.2` and `channel: experimental`, and `kubectl explain httproute.spec.rules.retry --recursive` answers with `attempts`, `backoff` and `codes` under `Support: Extended`, both read back from the API server into `crd-httproute.txt` in the run directory. That 500 and 503 are inside the set every implementation must support is recorded, with the file and the line numbers it was read at, in `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-pipeline/sources.md` §3. It is applied by `make retry-on ROUTE=<waypoint|ingress|egress>` and removed by `make retry-off`, both of which are `kubectl apply` of route objects rendered from `deploy/step-3-stress/retry/<route>/{off,on}` and filtered to their `HTTPRoute` documents; no image is built and no Deployment is rolled by either. **Stimulus and injection per route.** `waypoint`: one in-cluster loadgen Job to the worker Service, whose pod is ztunnel-captured, so the request crosses the worker's own istiod-driven agentgateway waypoint; the worker armed with `http503-before-dispatch` for the repetition's work item, which writes the arrival line and answers 503 before the A2A SDK sees the request, and disarms itself, so a second delivery is served. `ingress`: the out-of-cluster path, a `kind` port-forward to the ingress Service and one POST from the host addressed to the worker as `worker.lab.internal`, the same injection armed. The load client cannot be used off-cluster here, because it resolves the agent card and then sends to the in-cluster address the card advertises, so the POST is made by `curl` with no `--retry`, carrying the body shape `internal/a2areq` builds with a fresh JSON-RPC id and messageId, the identity headers every lab client sends, and `A2A-Version: 1.0`; the client line it writes is in each repetition's `client.jsonl` beside the request and response bodies. `egress`: one clean in-cluster loadgen Job to the worker, with the model endpoint armed `http500` for the work item; that arming is keyed by work item and is not taken, so a re-sent call is answered 500 as well. **Separately from the runs**, each proxy's own `/config_dump` was read once with the stanza on, through `kubectl port-forward deploy/<proxy> 15000`, which is the read-back the agentgateway documentation gives; that is the check that the proxy holds the policy and it is not evidence that the proxy fired it. One repetition of the collector's own span accounting was taken on both sides of a new `filter` processor that drops readiness-probe spans, added to `deploy/step-3-stress/otel-collector.yaml` in this task and applied with `kubectl -n telemetry apply -f` plus a restart of that Deployment alone. The worker gained a `MODEL_RETRIES` knob in this task; it was 0, its default, for every repetition here, and no other retry knob was set anywhere.
- Result: **all three routes fired the retry in 5 of 5, and every second delivery was byte-identical to the first.** Per route, with the config_dump read first and the counts after it. `waypoint`, `lab/agentgateway-waypoint`: **config_dump shows the policy, 1 retry policy** on the `lab/worker.0.0.mesh` route, rendered as `{"attempts": 1, "backoff": "100ms", "codes": ["503 Service Unavailable"]}`; **retried 5 of 5**; arrivals at the worker 2 in 5 of 5, the first answered 503 with `injection: http503-before-dispatch` and the second 200; identity across the two arrivals identical in 5 of 5 on the A2A `messageId`, the JSON-RPC `id`, `body_sha256` and `body_len` (292 bytes both times); `taskId` is empty on both arrivals, this being a first message, and is recorded as not comparable; executor entries **1**, model invocations **1**, client `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`. `ingress`, `agentgateway-system/agentgateway-ingress`: **config_dump shows the policy, 2 retry policies**, one on each of `lab/worker-ingress.00.http` and `lab/orchestrator-ingress.00.http`; **retried 5 of 5**; arrivals 2 in 5 of 5, 503 then 200; identity identical in 5 of 5 on all four fields (`body_len` 290 both times); executor entries **1**, model invocations **1**, client `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`. `egress`, `agentgateway-egress/agw-egress`: **config_dump shows the policy, 1 retry policy** on the `model-via-agw` route; **retried 5 of 5**; arrivals at the worker **1**, model invocations at the endpoint **2** in 5 of 5, both answered 500; identity across the two invocation lines identical in 5 of 5 on `messageId`, `taskId`, `caller` and `body_sha256`; executor entries **1**, client `task`/`TASK_STATE_FAILED` with `model call: status 500` on the execution ledger. **The gap between the two attempts matches the backoff**: waypoint 102–105 ms and ingress 100–104 ms between the two arrivals, and egress 303–314 ms between the two invocations, which is the model endpoint's own ~200 ms latency before it answers 500 plus the same ~100 ms. **Trace evidence**, from `spans.csv` per work item. On the two routes whose proxy exports, the retry is two backend spans under one route span: the ingress work item is **9 spans in 1 trace id** (`agentgateway-ingress`=3, `worker`=3, `agw-egress`=2, `mockllm`=1), the three ingress spans being one `POST /*` route span and two `POST worker.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080` client spans, the first parenting the worker's 503 and the second the worker's 200; the egress work item is **10 spans in 2 trace ids** (`loadgen`=2, `worker`=3, `agw-egress`=3, `mockllm`=2), the three egress spans being one `POST /*` and two `POST mockllm.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080`, each parenting one model invocation. The istiod-driven waypoint exports nothing, as Task 1 measured, so its retry shows in the shape Task 1 predicted would have to serve: the waypoint work item is **9 spans in 2 trace ids** (`loadgen`=2, `worker`=4, `agw-egress`=2, `mockllm`=1) in which **both of the worker's `POST /` server spans name the same parent span id, and that span id names no exported span** — one waypoint span issued both attempts. Every repetition's identity comparison, counts, client result and span count is one row of `summary.csv`. **The readiness-probe filter**: with the traces pipeline as Task 1 left it, 150 spans accepted and **150 exported** in 60 s with nothing in flight; with the `filter` processor in front of it, 150 accepted, 150 into the filter and **0 out of it, 0 exported** in the same window. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-gateway-retry-mechanics/` (`summary.csv`, one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json` and `spans.csv`, and for the ingress repetitions the `request.json` and `response.json` that were on the wire; `config-dump-waypoint.txt`, `config-dump-ingress.txt`, `config-dump-egress.txt`, `routes-on-<route>/routes.txt` and `routes-off-<route>/routes.txt` per route, `collector-span-rate.txt`, `control.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, `crd-httproute.txt`).
- Interpretation: as documented where a document exists, and the one place the documents are silent is answered by the counts. Gateway API v1.6.2 describes `attempts`, `codes` and `backoff` and says nothing about a request body; agentgateway's retry page gives the same three fields and the `/config_dump` read-back and says nothing about a body either. So whether a POST body survives a retry was an open question at these pins, and on all three routes it did: the second delivery carried the same `body_sha256` as the first in **15 of 15** repetitions, and on the two receiver-facing routes the same JSON-RPC `id` and the same A2A `messageId` with it. `body_len` was compared as well wherever it exists, which is the **10** receiver-facing repetitions, and was identical in all of them at 292 bytes on the waypoint route and 290 on the ingress route; the model endpoint's invocation ledger records no body length, so on the five egress repetitions that comparison was not taken and `summary.csv` carries it as not applicable. What that answers precisely is that the proxy had the whole body available to send again; whether it held it in a buffer or replayed it some other way is not something a ledger can see, and these bodies are 290 and 292 bytes, so nothing here says what a body larger than whatever the proxy is willing to hold would do. The result that was not safe to assume is the waypoint's. Istio's agentgateway page lists HTTPRoute among the resources it passes through but says nothing about the retry stanza specifically, and Task 1 had measured an `AgentgatewayPolicy` being accepted by agentgateway's controller for one of these waypoints while the proxy istiod actually programs held nothing of it. The two resources behave differently, and the difference is visible in the same `/config_dump` that showed the empty policy list at Task 1: the retry arrives on the route as an inline policy, and it fires. Reading the retry as a duplicate of work is wrong on two of these three routes and right on the third, and the difference is where the failure sat relative to the receiver's dispatch. On the waypoint and ingress routes the injected 503 is written after the arrival is counted and before the A2A SDK sees the request, so the first delivery did nothing except appear on the ingress ledger; the retry then produced one executor entry, one Task and one model invocation, and the client got a completed Task it would otherwise not have got. Those rows are a second delivery with no second unit of work. On the egress route the failure is at the far end of a call the executor had already started, so the retry produced a second model invocation carrying the same work item, the same Task id and the same bytes, and the endpoint saw the work twice while the client saw one failed Task. That is the shape A.3's R2 and the egress row have to classify, and it says the classification cannot be read off the layer alone: a gateway retry duplicates whatever the failed attempt had already done, which on this receiver depends on whether the failure was injected before or after dispatch. The counts also settle a smaller thing that the matrix needs: the backoff is honoured and is measured from the response rather than from the request, which is why the egress gap is the model's latency plus the backoff rather than the backoff alone.
- Follow-up: none. No document read in this session was contradicted by what was observed, and the one silence, on request-body buffering, is recorded above as a silence answered by counts rather than as a gap to file.

  Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-r1-go-http/`, `.../2026-09-09-a3-r1-go-sdk/`, `.../2026-09-09-a3-r1-py-http/`, `.../2026-09-09-a3-r1-py-sdk/`, each with `summary.csv` (20 rows, the fourteen columns named in `experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`), `knobs.txt`, `control.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, and one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json`, `spans.csv` and `attribution.txt`.
- Interpretation: on the counts alone this row reads as safe on both receivers and both layers — one Task, one model invocation, twenty of twenty, on every sub-row — because R1's injection is built to fail the first delivery before dispatch (`close-after-read` / `http503-before-dispatch`, both fired after the ingress ledger counts the arrival and before the SDK sees it), so the retry always fires into a receiver that never started work on the logical message. That is what the counts show, and it is the only shape R1 can produce here: the injection point is fixed. It is not the only shape a client retry with these knobs can produce. Both layers preserve the A2A `messageId` across the retry — measured here on all eighty work items, and by A.2 independently for both SDKs and both layers: byte-identical at the HTTP layer, same `messageId` under a new JSON-RPC id at the SDK layer — which is exactly the identity a receiver would need to deduplicate on, and A.1 measured that neither a2a-go v2.5.0 nor a2a-python 1.1.2 does: a second delivery of the same `messageId` that reaches dispatch is a second Task and a second model invocation, in 20 of 20, for M1 (exact transport replay) and M2 (same message, new RPC id), at both receivers. So the counterfactual the brief asks for is not a guess, it is A.1's own measured M1/M2 result carried across: had the first delivery of an R1 retry succeeded at the receiver rather than been refused before dispatch — a slow response the client gave up on and retried, say, rather than a connection close — the identical shape, a second dispatch, a second Task and a second model call for the one logical work item, with the client seeing only the final answer, is what the ledgers would show, on either layer, on either receiver. That is the reasoning behind **potentially dangerous** rather than **safe**: the classification is about what the layer can do to a side-effecting model call, not only about what this particular injection happened to test. The trace corroborates the layer of the retry — client-http, byte-identical, one client line; client-sdk, a new RPC id, two client lines — wherever a second receiver server span exists to compare one against, and, where it does not, from the nearest proxy that does. A receiver-side injection that resolves before the inner app's own OTel instrumentation runs, measured here at the Python receiver on both sub-rows from the middleware order in `agents/orchestrator/orchestrator/server.py` (the OTel auto-instrumentation attaches when `Starlette(routes=routes)` is constructed; `IngressMiddleware` is added afterwards and sits outermost), leaves nothing at the receiver to compare for the refused attempt. For the `sdk` sub-row that does not matter, since rule (a) — a new JSON-RPC id under one `messageId` — answers from the ledger before any span is examined. For the `http` sub-row it does matter, and the derivation's first pass returned `not-attributable` for exactly this reason; extended (this task, named fix above) with a fallback to the nearest exporting proxy's own inbound spans, it now reads `client-http` from the `agentgateway-ingress`'s two separate entries, the same "one entry per delivery" shape the Go receiver shows directly at its own server span. So both `http` sub-rows now read the same layer for the same reason — an HTTP-layer client retry — reached by two different vantage points because the two receivers instrument a refused delivery differently, not because the delivery was refused differently: the Go receiver's `otelhttp.Handler` wraps the whole mux (`agents/worker/main.go:153`), so it opens a span before `close-after-read` ever runs; the Python receiver's own middleware order does not, so a delivery `IngressMiddleware` refuses is visible one hop out, at the proxy, but not at the receiver. That is a lab wiring fact, not a difference in what either client or gateway did, and it is one this fallback should keep resolving correctly on R2 and R4, whenever the same injection mode fires at the Python receiver. The Python `sdk` sub-row's own single-loadgen-span trace is the same fact wearing a different mask, not a second one: `make export-trace` selects whole traces by the `lab.work_item` attribute, which no `loadgen` or proxy span ever carries in this row (0 of 180, 0 of 120, 0 of 160), so attempt 1's trace is retrieved only when some *other* service's span in it carries the attribute — which happens at the Go receiver, whose refused attempt still opens a `worker` server span, and does not happen at the Python receiver, whose refused attempt opens none. The rule (a) ledger check answers this sub-row before any of that matters for the label, so it does not change the classification either; it is recorded because the exported trace is not what a reader would assume it is (one span covering two attempts) but is worth stating correctly rather than leaving as an open question the fallback was never going to answer, since it is not a proxy-attribution question at all.
- Follow-up: none. The Python `http` sub-row's need for the proxy-span fallback and the Python `sdk` sub-row's single-span trace both trace to the same root fact — `IngressMiddleware` sits outside the OTel auto-instrumentation and answers a refused delivery before it opens a server span, a consequence of CLAUDE.md rule 5 (ledgers before agent logic) — surfaced through two different mechanisms: the derivation's need for a second receiver span to compare a parent against, and `make export-trace`'s selection of whole traces by an attribute only a receiver or the mock span ever carries. Neither is a defect in a2a-python, Starlette's instrumentation, or agentgateway; nothing here behaved unlike a document read in this session, and the harness fix is recorded as a named fix rather than a silent edit.

  | Gateway (R2) waypoint, Go receiver | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | potentially dangerous | 1 Task/1 call here only because the injection refuses the first delivery before dispatch; A.1 M1 measured 2/2 for a byte-identical second delivery that reaches dispatch |

  | Gateway (R2) waypoint, Python receiver | not applicable | — | — | — | — | not applicable | no `HTTPRoute` names the orchestrator Service as parent; this receiver's `SendMessage` POST enters through the agentgateway ingress, not its own waypoint (Task 3 baseline measurement); refused by the harness before anything is sent |
  | Gateway (R2) ingress, Python receiver | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | potentially dangerous | same reason as the Go rows; the byte-identical retry and the refusal-before-dispatch are identical on this receiver |
  | Gateway (R2) ingress-incluster, Python receiver | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | potentially dangerous | same reason |

This is the fallback's `gateway` branch that Task 4's report flagged as unexercised by any R1 row and asked this task to check; it fires correctly here, 20 of 20. 54 spans per work item (`agentgateway-ingress=3|agw-egress=2|mockllm=1|orchestrator=48`), 1 trace id (no `loadgen` and no card fetch, for the same reason as the Go `ingress` sub-row). `ingress-incluster` sub-row (an in-cluster loadgen Job): the identical shape — one `orchestrator POST /` entry span, two `agentgateway-ingress` upstream spans sharing one parent, `layer=gateway` in 20 of 20 via the same fallback branch — plus a `loadgen` client span and a card-fetch trace this time, since the stimulus is loadgen rather than `curl`: 59 spans per work item (`agentgateway-ingress=3|agw-egress=2|loadgen=2|mockllm=1|orchestrator=51`), 2 trace ids.

  **Request-body buffering.** Neither Gateway API v1.6.2 nor agentgateway's own retry documentation says anything about how a POST body survives a retry attempt, which Task 2's entry already established and this row's counts confirm rather than newly discover: the second arrival was byte-identical to the first in all 80 of 80 repetitions here, including the two sub-rows where the first delivery reached the proxy over one TCP connection and the retry over the same one (loadgen's `waypoint` and `ingress-incluster` sub-rows) and the two where a single `curl` process without `--retry` sent one request and the gateway alone produced the second (Go and Python `ingress`). So the proxy had the whole body available to re-send in every shape this row tested; whether it held the request in a buffer, replayed it from some other internal representation, or something else again is not something a ledger or a `/config_dump` read can distinguish, and these bodies (302–322 bytes) say nothing about a body large enough to test a buffer's limit. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-r2-go-waypoint/`, `.../2026-09-09-a3-r2-go-ingress/`, `.../2026-09-09-a3-r2-py-ingress/`, `.../2026-09-09-a3-r2-py-ingress-incluster/`, each with `summary.csv` (20 rows, the fourteen columns named in `experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`), `knobs.txt`, `control.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, `routes.txt`, `config-dump-<route>.txt`, and one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl` (plus `request.json`/`response.json` on the `curl` sub-rows), `trace.json`, `spans.csv` and `attribution.txt`.

- Interpretation: a gateway-level `HTTPRoute` retry preserves A2A message identity and body at these pins — byte-identical body, `messageId` and JSON-RPC `id` in 80 of 80, on both routes, at both receivers, whichever process sent the original request — and on the counts alone every sub-row reads as safe: one Task, one model invocation, twenty of twenty. That reading is an artefact of where this row's injection sits, not of what the layer can do to a side-effecting call, and the classification follows A.1's own measured counterfactual rather than a guess: `http503-before-dispatch` refuses the first delivery before the A2A SDK ever sees it, so the retry is the only delivery that does any work, but the shape of the two arrivals — exact transport replay, same body, same `messageId`, same JSON-RPC `id` — is precisely A.1's M1, and A.1 measured that a byte-identical second delivery which *does* reach dispatch is a second Task and a second model invocation, 20 of 20, at both receivers. So a gateway retry that fires after a delivery whose response was merely lost or delayed, rather than refused pre-dispatch, would duplicate the model call exactly as M1 recorded; nothing about the retry-layer mechanics changes that outcome, since the gateway's job is precisely to make the second delivery indistinguishable from the first. That is **potentially dangerous** rather than **safe**, on every one of the four applicable sub-rows, for the same one-line reason.

  Task 2 had already measured that a gateway retry is not automatically duplicated work when the failure precedes dispatch, and this row adds the receiver-instrumentation half of that picture that Task 4 first found on the client layer and flagged for this row to check: at the Python receiver, a pre-dispatch refusal is invisible to the receiver's own OTel instrumentation because `IngressMiddleware` sits outside the Starlette app it wraps and answers before that app's instrumentation ever runs, so every `ingress`-route sub-row on this receiver is attributed through the proxy fallback rather than through the receiver's own server spans. That fallback's `gateway` branch — one proxy entry carrying two upstream attempts — had not been exercised by any row before this task (R1 only exercised its `client-http` branch, on a route with no route-level retry on), and it read correctly here in 40 of 40 Python work items across both `ingress` sub-rows, which is the check Task 4's report asked for. The Go `waypoint` and `ingress` sub-rows attribute by two different rules of the same derivation — one shared parent span id at the waypoint, two client spans sharing one grandparent at the ingress — and both land on `gateway` for the reason each route's own proxy topology gives, not because either rule assumes the answer. One thing the `ingress` sub-rows (both receivers) show plainly at the client: the out-of-cluster `curl` sender, with no `--retry` of its own, received exactly one HTTP response, `200`/`task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, for a request that the ingress route answered `503` on its first attempt and `200` on its second — the retry is complete and invisible above the gateway, which is the same shape Task 2 measured and this row confirms holds under R2's own injection and counting rules rather than only under the mechanics script's.

- Follow-up: none. No document read in this session was contradicted by what was observed, the request-body-buffering silence is recorded as a silence answered by counts (as Task 2's entry did), and the Python `waypoint` sub-row's non-applicability is a topology fact already established and re-verified here, not a new finding.

## Gate 3 / both receivers / A.3 R3 — What does an application/model-client retry duplicate below the A2A layer?
- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.2 openai-python=3.9.0
- Environment: kind
- Method: `make matrix RUN=R3 RECEIVER=go REPS=20` and `make matrix RUN=R3 RECEIVER=py REPS=20` (`experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`), on 2026-09-09/10, each counted invocation preceded by its own one-repetition dry run under its own nonce (directory deleted), twenty repetitions per receiver, forty counted work items in all, RUN_IDs 235451 (go) and 000624 (py), neither reused. Telemetry pins: collector=otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.160.0, jaeger=jaegertracing/jaeger:2.20.0, prometheus=prom/prometheus:v3.14.0, operator=v0.158.0 (Helm chart 0.122.0), otel-go=v1.46.0, otel-go-contrib=v0.71.0, and for the Python agent the OpenTelemetry distro 0.65b0. The certificate check ran first on every invocation and found `VALID CERT true` for `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/lab/sa/default`, so `ztunnel` was not restarted on any of them; both committed `certificates.txt` files record `NOT AFTER 2026-09-10T19:19:14Z` for that identity (the leaf had rotated since R2's entry, which is why this figure differs from earlier Gate 3 rows).

  R3 switches on only the receiver's own model-client retry, nothing above it: worker `MODEL_RETRIES=1` (`httpclient.NewRetryingOn(timeout, 1, RetryOnTransportOr503)`, re-sending the same bytes on a transport error or on an HTTP 503 response and on no other status, per `internal/httpclient/httpclient.go`), orchestrator `MODEL_MAX_RETRIES=1` (`openai.AsyncOpenAI`'s own retry, default 0 in this lab). Both set by `kubectl set env` on the Deployment for the run, recorded and restored; the Python receiver's code has not changed since Task 1, so `kubectl set env` needed no rebuild there. Route retries stayed off throughout (0 stanzas asserted before and after both invocations, on all four routes this lab patches), and no `CLIENT_*` variable reached either Job — client and gateway layers both out, so a second model invocation here can only be this row's own knob. Both receivers' own injection stayed clean: the worker's and orchestrator's control endpoints were reset and never armed for this row.

  The mock is armed by invocation count, not by work item: `POST /control/inject {"mode":"close","at_count":1}` after a `POST /control/reset` before every repetition. Read from `fixtures/mockllm/injection.go` and `server.go`: `invocationCount` is one counter, global to the mock process, incremented by `nextInvocationCount()` on every `/v1/chat/completions` call and zeroed only by `/control/reset`; `fires(count, lwi)` matches `at_count` by exact equality (`count == cfg.AtCount`), 1-indexed since the last reset, so arming `at_count:1` after a reset fails exactly the first call on that counter and lets every later one succeed. Arming by `lwi` instead (as the baseline and egress rows do) would fire on every call carrying that identity, including the retried one, since a work-item-keyed injection does not distinguish which attempt of a given work item it is checking — which is why R3 (and R4, composed, not run in this task) both key the mock by `at_count`: R3's own retry could not otherwise succeed. The harness resets both injectors before every repetition, so `at_count:1` is always that repetition's own first call, never a previous repetition's.
