  **Named fix, this task, in three rounds.** `MODEL_RETRIES=1` was set on the live Deployment and read back correctly (`kubectl set env` restarts the pod, which is all that command does), but the running worker image predated the code that reads that variable: `agents/worker/main.go`'s `modelRetries()` landed in Task 2 (`f84cbf8`), one commit after the worker image then running was last built (Task 1's `9ba9983`; Task 2's own report states plainly that "`make step-3` was not run" after adding it). `kubectl set env` restarts a pod onto whatever image the Deployment already names; it does not rebuild anything, so the variable reached a binary that never checks for it. Run `220952` showed `invocations=1` in every one of the 20 work items — the retry never fired. That is not a finding about `a2a-go`'s or the model client's own retry logic; it is a stale-image artefact, discarded rather than written up, per rule 3, and the worker image was rebuilt and reloaded into the cluster's `kind` node from a checkout at HEAD.

  The first version of the guard compared the running Deployment's image against what `ko build --push=false` resolves from the checkout right now, and that was itself wrong: `ko`'s own tag is not a pure content hash of the Go source — two builds of byte-identical code, run about forty minutes apart in this same session, resolved to two different tags for the worker (`kind.local/worker-…:7f5add70…` then `kind.local/worker-…:bdf46076…`), almost certainly because the OCI image's own `Created` field defaults to build wall-clock time. That check would have refused every future row once enough time had passed, whichever receiver it ran against and whether or not the code had actually changed. It was caught before it reached a committed run and replaced with a check keyed on ReplicaSet history instead of a second build: `kubectl set env` changes a Deployment's pod template without ever touching its `image:` field, so the *earliest* ReplicaSet still carrying the declared image marks when that image was truly last built — an env-only restart creates a new ReplicaSet with the *same* image string, so it should not move that timestamp forward. That second version is what both committed runs' `knobs.txt` carry, and it passed correctly for both: it is not wrong about `220952`, `235451` or `000624`.

  It has a real flaw, found by review rather than by this task, and it is corrected here rather than left standing: Kubernetes prunes ReplicaSets past `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10), and once the ReplicaSet that first carried a given image is pruned, the next-surviving one with that same image is *later* — which only ever makes "a commit lands after the deploy" true *less* often. The guard degrades toward **passing** a stale image as history churns, not toward refusing one, and the drift is not hypothetical: at review time the worker Deployment was at revision 37 with only 2 of 11 surviving ReplicaSets carrying its current image, a margin of about nine ReplicaSets before this exact mechanism would have started passing the very bug it exists to catch. Replaced, ruled by the team lead: every step target that runs `ko apply` (`step-1`, `step-2`, `step-2b`, `step-2c`, `step-3`) now also annotates the worker and mock Deployments with `lab.agent-mesh/go-sources=<hash>` (`GO_SOURCES_HASH` in the Makefile — a content hash of the tracked Go sources under `agents/worker`, `fixtures/mockllm`, `internal/`, `go.mod` and `go.sum`, test files excluded since `ko` does not compile them). `image_fresh_or_die()` now recomputes that same hash from the checkout with the same command and refuses unless each Deployment's own annotation matches it exactly, or if the checkout carries an uncommitted change under those paths, or if the hash cannot be computed at all — nothing in this version depends on elapsed time, ReplicaSet count, or a second build, so nothing in it can drift the way the first two versions did. It is read-only against the cluster and records the checkout hash, each Deployment's annotation, and every one of its running pods' own `imageID` in `knobs.txt`.

  Both committed runs (`235451` go, `000624` py) predate this third version: their own `knobs.txt` carry the *second* version's output (the ReplicaSet-timestamp check, which passed correctly for both), not this one's. Each run's own `cluster-versions.txt` records the ko image reference both Deployments ran under at the time (`kind.local/worker-…:7f5add70…`, `kind.local/mockllm-…:44082d5b…`); the imageIDs those references resolve to, worker `sha256:931e1d24…` and mock `sha256:4a5a227a…`, were read back live after both counted runs and appended to each `cluster-versions.txt` as a dated block (`read back after the run, controller ruling`), alongside both Deployments' `lab.agent-mesh/go-sources` annotation. That block also shows why the two pods' own creation timestamps do not agree: the mock pod's matches the 19:37Z build exactly, since nothing in this task ever sets a knob on it, while the worker pod's is later, from this same task's own subsequent `kubectl set env`/`kubectl annotate` calls — its `imageID` is unchanged across every one of those restarts, which is the whole point of the distinction this guard's second and third versions were built to make. Both images were built by `make step-3` at 19:37Z on 2026-09-09 from a tree whose Go sources are confirmed identical to this entry's own HEAD (`git diff --stat 6f9f6cb..HEAD -- agents/worker fixtures/mockllm internal go.mod go.sum` is empty — no commit in this task touched those paths), and both Deployments have since been stamped with that tree's hash and verified to pass the third version live. This is the only change made to `experiments/gate3-matrix.sh` for this task, beyond the guard's own two prior, superseded versions kept as comments explaining why each was replaced; every other line the row exercises is exactly what Task 3 built.

  Stimulus: an in-cluster loadgen Job through each receiver's own path — direct to the worker Service, crossing its own istiod-driven waypoint, for the Go receiver; to the orchestrator Service, crossing the agentgateway ingress its card advertises, for the Python receiver, run in model mode (`DOWNSTREAM_A2A_URL` read off the live Deployment as `http://worker.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080`, unset for the run, confirmed unset live after the rollout, restored and confirmed live again on exit). Counting follows the Gate 2/3 rule: deliveries are arrival-phase ingress lines with `method == "SendMessage"`; dispatched are execution `execute` lines; distinct `messageId`s and Tasks come from the same two ledgers; invocations are the mock's lines excluding `stale-closed`; `client_result` is loadgen's own client line. `second_delivery_layer` is derived by `experiments/lib/derive-layer.sh` from each repetition's own ledgers and trace alone.

- Result: identical across all twenty repetitions on each receiver, and identical between the two receivers on every ledger count: deliveries **1**, dispatched **1**, distinct `messageId`s **1**, Tasks created **1**, model invocations **2**, client result `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, in 20 of 20 on both. The results-table line:

  | Retry layer | Deliveries at B (pre-dispatch) | Dispatched by A2A server | Distinct `messageId`s | Tasks created | Model invocations | Classification | Reason |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
  | Model client (R3), Go receiver | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | potentially dangerous | one Task and one delivery, both counted once, hide two model invocations under the same identity |
  | Model client (R3), Python receiver | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | potentially dangerous | same reason as the Go row; identical counts, same identity carried across both invocations |

  Identity across the two invocations, checked directly against every work item's own `invocation.jsonl` rather than only against `summary.csv`: 40 of 40 show the same `logical_work_item_id`, the same `messageId` and the same `taskId` on both lines, the first `injection:"close" outcome:"closed"`, the second `injection:"none" outcome:"ok"`, on both receivers.

  **Go receiver.** The mock's `close` reaches the egress waypoint's own hop as a 503, the same way the baseline measured it (`model call: status 503`), and `httpclient.NewRetryingOn`'s `RetryOnTransportOr503` mode re-sends on exactly that status. The worker's own client span does not show the intermediate 503 directly, because `internal/otel.Transport` wraps *outside* `retryTransport` (`agents/worker/main.go`: `modelHTTP.Transport = labotel.Transport(modelHTTP.Transport)`, applied after the retrying client is built), so the two internal round trips are invisible to OpenTelemetry and produce one `worker HTTP POST` client span covering the whole exchange, ending at its final, successful status (`200`, 20 of 20) — the same wrapping-order fact Task 4 found for loadgen's own `http` sub-row. What does show the retry is the egress hop underneath that one span: two separate `agw-egress POST /*` entries, the first lasting 342–1535 µs (n=20, well under the mock's own ~200 ms latency, consistent with an immediate connection close rather than a served response) and the second the full ~200 ms mock latency, both nested under the same worker client span. `layer=model-client` in 20 of 20, from the ledger rule alone (two invocations under one execution) and corroborated by the trace's own count of two egress entries for one delivery. 11 spans per work item (`agw-egress=4|loadgen=2|mockllm=2|worker=3`).

  **Python receiver.** The mock's `close` reaches the orchestrator's own outbound span directly as a 503 — measured, not inferred: the orchestrator's first `POST` client span carries `http_status=503` in 20 of 20, its second `http_status=200`, both under the same execution, because the httpx instrumentation (`opentelemetry.instrumentation.httpx`) opens one span per HTTP request and `openai.AsyncOpenAI`'s retry loop issues two requests above that instrumented transport, unlike the Go worker's single-span shape, where the retry loops inside the instrumented transport. openai-python 3.9.0's own retry conditions were read from the pinned source in this session (`_base_client.py` at the `v3.9.0` tag, `AsyncAPIClient._request`): once a response is received, `_should_retry()` retries only on an `x-should-retry: true` response header, or HTTP status 408, 409, 429, or any status **≥ 500**, and on no other status; a raised exception with no response at all (a timeout, or any other exception that is not itself an `OpenAIError`) is retried unconditionally while `remaining_retries > 0`, with `APIConnectionError`'s own default message ("Connection error.", from `_exceptions.py`) reserved for the case retries are exhausted with no response ever received. The measured `http_status=503` on the failed attempt's own span places this row's retry squarely on the first path — the "≥500" branch of `_should_retry()` — not the generic-exception branch: the injected failure, once the egress waypoint has converted it, is one of the status codes openai's own retry logic explicitly covers, and `MODEL_MAX_RETRIES=1` is exactly the count needed to cover the one failure this row injects. `layer=model-client` in 20 of 20, from the ledger rule and from the trace's own count of two calls entering the egress waypoint for one delivery. 62 spans per work item (`agentgateway-ingress=2|agw-egress=4|loadgen=2|mockllm=2|orchestrator=52`).

  Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-r3-go/` and `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-a3-r3-py/` (the run crossed midnight local between the two invocations), each with `summary.csv` (20 rows, the fourteen columns named in `experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`), `knobs.txt` (including the image-freshness guard's second-version output, above), `control.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, and one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json`, `spans.csv` and `attribution.txt`.

- Interpretation: at both receivers a model-client retry duplicates the model call while leaving every A2A-layer count exactly as a single, successful delivery would: one arrival, one dispatch, one Task, one completed result. That is what makes this row's shape different from R1 and R2 rather than merely another **potentially dangerous** entry with the same reason — in R1 and R2 the second delivery was visible at the pre-dispatch ledger (deliveries=2) even though the injection kept it from becoming a second Task; here the ingress and execution ledgers show no evidence whatsoever that a retry happened, and only the invocation ledger — one layer below where CLAUDE.md rule 5 puts the ledgers this lab builds first — records the second call. A caller, or an operator, watching only the A2A-level ledgers or the Task's own state transitions would see one clean delivery and never learn that the model was invoked twice for it. Both SDKs' own retry conditions point at the same trigger, and neither is a guess: the Go worker's `httpclient.NewRetryingOn(..., RetryOnTransportOr503)` and openai-python 3.9.0's `_should_retry()` (fetched from the pinned source in this session) both re-send on an HTTP 503, and the mock's `close`, once the egress waypoint converts it (measured directly on the orchestrator's own span, and consistent with the baseline's identical measurement plus the Go worker's own first-attempt duration, well under the mock's normal latency), lands on exactly that status at both receivers — so this row's retry is not an edge case relative to what the baseline already showed the injection produces, it is the same converted failure, now with a knob that answers it. The classification is **potentially dangerous** rather than **safe**: this lab's model endpoint is a stateless text completion with no side effect to duplicate, but the shape measured here — one Task, one delivery, two calls to whatever backs the model — is exactly the shape that would double a real side effect (a tool call, a write, a charge) behind an agent's own model-client retry, with nothing at the A2A layer to reveal it, and a lower detection floor than R1 or R2 because even the delivery count stays at one. The image-staleness fact this task found and fixed (Named fix, above) is a lab operational finding, not a finding about either SDK, the gateway, or the model client, and it changed no count in this entry; it is recorded here because it is exactly the kind of quiet, undetected non-effect this row's own classification warns about, one layer further down the same stack.

- Follow-up: none. Both retry conditions were read from documents fetched in this session (`internal/httpclient/httpclient.go` in this repository; `_base_client.py` and `_exceptions.py` at the `openai-python` `v3.9.0` tag) rather than assumed, the injected failure was confirmed, not guessed, to be one each retry logic covers, and nothing here behaved unlike what was read. The stale worker image is a lab process gap in this task's own commit sequencing, not a project gap in `a2a-go`, `a2a-python`, `openai-python`, or agentgateway, so no `docs/upstream/` draft applies; it is carried forward as a standing check in the harness instead.

## Gate 3 / both receivers / A.3 R4 — What happens when policies compose?
- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.2 openai-python=3.9.0
- Environment: kind
- Method: `make matrix RUN=R4 RECEIVER=go REPS=20` and `make matrix RUN=R4 RECEIVER=py REPS=20` (`experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`, reused unchanged — running this row needed no harness edit; `git diff 734b1a4..HEAD -- experiments/gate3-matrix.sh experiments/lib Makefile deploy` is empty), two invocations on 2026-09-09/10, each preceded by its own one-repetition dry run under the invocation's own wall-clock `RUN_ID` nonce (`-dry` suffix, directory deleted by the harness), twenty counted repetitions after it, forty counted work items in all, RUN_IDs `005741` (go) and `010852` (py), neither reused and neither appearing in any earlier run. Telemetry pins: collector=otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.160.0, jaeger=jaegertracing/jaeger:2.20.0, prometheus=prom/prometheus:v3.14.0, operator=v0.158.0 (Helm chart 0.122.0), otel-go=v1.46.0, otel-go-contrib=v0.71.0, and for the Python agent the OpenTelemetry distro 0.65b0. The certificate check ran first on both invocations and found `VALID CERT true` for `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/lab/sa/default`, valid until `2026-09-10T19:19:14Z`, so `ztunnel` was not restarted on either (`certificates.txt`). The image-freshness guard passed before either run's first stimulus, on both Deployments and on both invocations: checkout Go-sources hash `dc72c724b8308f76baa9f742aa5a7c7086d5d260` equal to the `lab.agent-mesh/go-sources` annotation on `deployment/worker` and `deployment/mockllm`, with the running pods' `imageID`s `sha256:931e1d24…` (worker) and `sha256:4a5a227a…` (mock) recorded in each run's own `knobs.txt`; `make step-3` was neither needed nor run.

  **What R4 composes, and which knobs carried each layer.** All three of the proposal's R4 columns are on at once. The client's HTTP layer: `CLIENT_RETRIES=1 CLIENT_RETRY_ON=transport+503` rendered into the loadgen Job, the byte-identical resend-on-503 A.2 measured, asserted absent as a `CLIENT_*` variable on every Deployment before each invocation. The receiver's model client: `MODEL_RETRIES=1` on `deployment/worker` (`httpclient.NewRetryingOn(timeout, 1, RetryOnTransportOr503)`) and `MODEL_MAX_RETRIES=1` on `deployment/orchestrator` (`openai.AsyncOpenAI`'s own retry), each read off the live Deployment before the run, set by `kubectl set env`, confirmed live after the rollout, restored and confirmed live again on exit. The gateway: one `HTTPRoute` retry stanza set (`retry: {attempts: 1, codes: [503], backoff: 100ms}`), per-route and cluster-wide counts both asserted equal to the row's expectation before anything was sent, and the live route objects read back into `routes.txt`. **Which gateway that is differs by receiver, per the controller's ruling after Task 3:** for the Go receiver it is the `waypoint` route set, one stanza on `lab/worker`, the istiod-driven agentgateway waypoint the in-cluster loadgen Job's request actually crosses; for the Python receiver it is the `ingress` route set, two stanzas, on `lab/worker-ingress` and `lab/orchestrator-ingress`, because no `HTTPRoute` names the orchestrator Service as its parent and that receiver's `SendMessage` POST enters through the agentgateway ingress its card advertises (Task 3's baseline measurement, re-verified in Task 5). The reason the substitution matters more here than in R2 is that an inert gateway in a composition row does not read as "the gateway did not retry"; it reads as "the layers did not compose". The harness refuses `ROUTE=waypoint` for the Python receiver before anything is sent, whatever row asks for it.

  **The injections armed, and the order in which each layer was given a chance to retry.** Two failures were armed per repetition, each scoped to that repetition alone, and both injectors were reset before and after every one of them (`control.txt`, 42 arms and 111 resets per invocation, every one answering `204`). First, the receiver's own `http503-before-dispatch`, armed by work item at `POST <receiver>/control/inject`. `close-after-read` is not used in this row, although it is what R1 injects at the Go receiver. Two reasons, and only the first is a measurement of this lab's own: the Python receiver refuses that mode with HTTP 400 (ASGI has no portable connection hijack), which is the harness's recorded reason for using `http503-before-dispatch` at every receiver-injecting row; and the gateway's retry policy matches on a response code (`codes: [503]`), while what a connection close presents to a route retry is not something this lab has counted — Gate 2 measured only that the istiod-driven waypoint converts a receiver's close into a synthesised 503 for the *client* (`experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a2-go-http/waypoint-503-probe.txt`), not that a route retry fires on that synthesis. Injecting the status the policy is known to match keeps the composition's gateway layer live rather than resting the row on a conversion nothing here has measured. A receiver holds one armed mode per work item (`agents/worker/control.go`, `agents/orchestrator/orchestrator/control.py`), so the one 503 stands for both R1's and R2's receiver-side injection; the harness records that in `knobs.txt` as its own injection note and in each row's `notes`. The armed mode fires once and disarms itself (`injector.take`), so it refuses exactly the first delivery of that work item and every later delivery is served. Second, the model endpoint's `close`, armed by invocation count, `{"mode":"close","at_count":1}`, after a reset. Read from `fixtures/mockllm/injection.go` and `server.go`: `invocationCount` is one counter global to the mock process, incremented on every `/v1/chat/completions` call and zeroed only by `/control/reset`; `fires(count, lwi)` matches `at_count` by exact equality, 1-indexed since that reset, and `newInjectionConfig` requires exactly one of `at_count` or `lwi` and rejects `at_count < 1`. The harness resets both injectors before every repetition, so `at_count:1` fails exactly that repetition's own first model call and lets the retry succeed; a work-item-keyed arming would have failed both attempts, which is why R3 and R4 key the mock by count.

  So the three layers sit on two hops, and only one of the two hops carries more than one retrying layer. On the **A2A delivery hop** (loadgen → gateway → receiver) two retrying layers are armed and one failure is injected, and the gateway is the inner of the two: it sees the receiver's 503 first and gets the first chance; the client's HTTP layer gets its chance second, and only on whatever status or transport error finally reaches it. On the **model hop** (receiver → egress waypoint → mock) exactly one retrying layer is armed — the receiver's own model client. R4 puts no stanza on the egress route (that is Task 8's own row), so on that hop nothing above the model client could have contested the failure. Both hops' failures reach their retrying layer as an HTTP 503: the receiver answers one itself, and the egress waypoint converts the mock's connection close into one, which the baseline and R3 both measured.

  Stimulus: an in-cluster loadgen Job through each receiver's own path, as every earlier in-cluster row used it — direct to the worker Service, crossing the worker's istiod-driven waypoint, for the Go receiver; to the orchestrator Service, whose card advertises `PUBLIC_URL`, so the card fetch crosses the orchestrator's waypoint and the `SendMessage` POST enters through the agentgateway ingress, for the Python receiver, which ran in model mode (`DOWNSTREAM_A2A_URL` read off the live Deployment as `http://worker.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080`, unset for the run, confirmed unset live after the rollout, restored and confirmed live again on exit, `knobs.txt`). All 40 loadgen Jobs reached `Complete`; none reached `Failed`. Counting follows the Gate 2/3 rule: deliveries are the receiver's own arrival-phase ingress lines with `method == "SendMessage"`; dispatched are execution `execute` lines; distinct `messageId`s and Tasks come from the same two ledgers; invocations are the mock's lines excluding `stale-closed`; `client_result` is loadgen's own client line(s). Per repetition, `make ledgers` two seconds after the client returned and `make export-trace` eight seconds after that, both inside the run because the batch span processors flush on a timer and the trace backend stores in memory. `second_delivery_layer` is derived by `experiments/lib/derive-layer.sh` from each repetition's own ledgers and trace alone, unchanged since Task 4's fix round 1: no knob value reaches it, so a row cannot be labelled by what it was expected to do.

  **One property of that derivation this row is the first to meet.** It emits a single `layer=` line, and its rules are ordered: a second delivery (rule (b)) is decided before a second model call (rule (c)). R4 is the first row where one work item carries both, so `summary.csv`'s `second_delivery_layer` column names the delivery hop only, and reads `gateway` in all 40. The model hop is attributed from the same `attribution.txt`, which prints rule (c)'s own two inputs for every work item whatever label it chose — `calls that entered the egress waypoint` and `upstream attempts the egress waypoint made` — so the second attribution below is rule (c) applied to the evidence the committed file already carries, not a second derivation and not a change to the library.

- Result: **identical across all twenty repetitions on each receiver, and identical between the two receivers on every ledger column**: deliveries **2**, dispatched **1**, distinct `messageId`s **1**, Tasks created **1**, model invocations **2**, client result `task`/`TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, one client line, in 20 of 20 on both. No `job_failed`, no `ledgers_rc`, no `export_trace_rc` on any of the 40 work items. The results-table line, per receiver:

  | Retry layer | Deliveries at B (pre-dispatch) | Dispatched by A2A server | Distinct `messageId`s | Tasks created | Model invocations | Classification | Reason |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
  | Composed (R4), Go receiver | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | potentially dangerous | two layers fired for one stimulus — a second byte-identical delivery and a second model call under one `taskId` and one `messageId` — while the client saw one line and the execution ledger one dispatch |
  | Composed (R4), Python receiver | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | potentially dangerous | same reason as the Go row; identical counts, and the same one Task carrying two model invocations |

  **The two arrivals are byte-identical in 40 of 40**, recomputed independently from each work item's own `ingress.jsonl` rather than read from `summary.csv`: one distinct `messageId`, one JSON-RPC `id`, one `body_sha256`, one `body_len` (286 bytes, the same on both receivers because both runs' work-item ids are 19 characters and the body carries the id twice) and `a2a_version` `1.0` across each work item's two arrival lines. The first arrival's response line carries `status: 503` and `injection: http503-before-dispatch`; the second carries `status: 200` and no injection, in 40 of 40. The gap between the two arrivals matches the stanza's 100 ms backoff on both receivers: Go 100.6–104.5 ms, Python 101.1–109.5 ms (n=20 each, from `ts_arrival`). **The dispatch is the second delivery's**, checked by timestamp in 40 of 40: the single execution `execute` line falls after both arrival lines, so the refused first delivery produced no dispatch, no Task and no model call of its own.

  **The two model invocations carry one identity** in 40 of 40, checked directly against every work item's own `invocation.jsonl`: the same `logical_work_item_id`, `messageId`, `taskId` and `body_sha256` on both lines, `caller` `worker` and `orchestrator` respectively, the first `injection: "close"` `outcome: "closed"`, the second `injection: "none"` `outcome: "ok"`.

  **The client's own HTTP retry never fired, on either receiver.** Three facts say so together and none of them alone: the receiver's pre-dispatch ledger counted two arrivals, not three; loadgen wrote exactly one client line, at attempt 1, with no error, in 40 of 40; and loadgen's own `HTTP POST` client span carries `http_status` 200 in 40 of 40. The knob was on and rendered into every Job (`CLIENT_RETRIES=1 CLIENT_RETRY_ON=transport+503`, recorded in each `knobs.txt`); it had nothing to fire on, because the gateway's own retry answered the 503 below it and returned a 200 upward. The composition's whole cost showed at the client only as latency: the one `HTTP POST` span measures 306.9–314.9 ms at the Go receiver and 701.8–823.7 ms at the Python one (n=20 each), against a mock latency of about 200 ms per served call.

  **Go receiver — trace evidence** (`attribution.txt` per work item, all twenty identical): 12 spans across 2 trace ids per work item, by service `agw-egress`=4, `loadgen`=2, `mockllm`=2, `worker`=4. *The second delivery is the gateway's*, `layer=gateway` in 20 of 20 from the ledger-first rule's shared-parent branch: the two `worker POST /` server spans name **one** parent span id in every work item (`a3m-r4-go-005741-01`: both name `5311b7080348b562`), itself dangling, which is the istiod-driven waypoint reading the trace context and exporting nothing — the same "one proxy span issued both attempts" shape Task 2 measured on this route and R2 counted 20 of 20. The two server spans carry `http_status` 503 then 200 in 20 of 20, the first 40–68 µs and the second 203.6–211.1 ms (n=20), the refused delivery answered before any work started and the served one covering the whole downstream exchange. *The second model call is the receiver's model client*, by rule (c) applied to the same file: **two** calls entered the egress waypoint per work item, with two upstream attempts pooled one per entry, in 20 of 20, which is rule (c)'s `model-client` branch and not its `gateway` one (that would need a single entry carrying two attempts). Both egress entries hang under **one** `worker HTTP POST` client span (202.5–209.6 ms, `http_status` 200, exactly one per work item), because `internal/otel.Transport` wraps outside `retryTransport` in `agents/worker/main.go`, so the two internal round trips are invisible to OpenTelemetry at the worker itself — the same wrapping-order fact R3 recorded. What separates them underneath is the egress hop: the first entry lasts 390–779 µs and the second 200.9–206.7 ms (n=20), the first far under the mock's own latency and consistent with an immediate connection close, the second a served call.

  **Python receiver — trace evidence**, all twenty identical: 63 spans across 2 trace ids per work item, by service `agentgateway-ingress`=3, `agw-egress`=4, `loadgen`=2, `mockllm`=2, `orchestrator`=52. *The second delivery is the gateway's*, `layer=gateway` in 20 of 20, reached through the proxy fallback Task 4 added rather than the direct branch: only **one** `orchestrator POST /` server span exists per work item, because `IngressMiddleware.__call__` answers the first delivery's `http503-before-dispatch` with a raw ASGI `send()` and returns without calling the inner, OTel-instrumented Starlette app (`agents/orchestrator/orchestrator/server.py:36-37`, `agents/orchestrator/orchestrator/ledger.py:107-143`, the code fact Task 4 established and R2 measured again). With fewer receiver entry spans than deliveries the derivation falls back to the nearest proxy that did export one, named from the surviving entry's own parent: the `agentgateway-ingress`, which shows **one** inbound `POST /*` route span carrying **two** upstream `POST orchestrator.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080` client spans, in 20 of 20 (`a3m-r4-py-010852-01`: route span `c2a8a59b1f30ec5d`, upstream spans `cd5171fe4b5184f8` at 580 µs, the refused attempt, and `ddacaf3c60440a13` at 720.6 ms, the served one; across the twenty, 490–646 µs and 596.0–720.6 ms). *The second model call is the receiver's model client*, again by rule (c): **two** calls entered the egress waypoint per work item, 20 of 20. Here the two attempts are visible at the receiver itself, unlike at the Go receiver, and the trace's own scope names say which library drew them rather than leaving it to be inferred: both spans are emitted by `opentelemetry.instrumentation.httpx` 0.65b0, one per HTTP request, in 20 of 20. `openai.AsyncOpenAI`'s retry loop sits above that instrumented transport and issues two requests through it, so each attempt gets a span of its own; the two sibling `POST` spans carry `http_status` 503 then 200 and are the parents of the two egress entries. The egress hop shows the same split as the Go receiver: first entry 380–516 µs, second 201.3–210.4 ms (n=20).

  Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-a3-r4-go/` and `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-a3-r4-py/`, each with `summary.csv` (20 rows, the fourteen columns named in `experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`), `knobs.txt` (including the image-freshness guard's output and the before and after states), `control.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, `routes.txt` and `routes-off/routes.txt`, and one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json`, `spans.csv` and `attribution.txt`.

- Interpretation: composing all three layers produced two duplications for one stimulus, not three and not a product of the three: one extra delivery and one extra model call, at both receivers, in 20 of 20. That is what the counts say and it follows from where each failure was answered rather than from the number of knobs switched on. Each injected failure was taken by the innermost retrying layer that could see it, and the layer above that one saw a success and had nothing to act on: the gateway answered the receiver's 503 and handed the client a 200, so the client's HTTP retry — armed, rendered into every Job, and asserted on — never fired; the receiver's model client answered the egress waypoint's converted 503 and completed its Task, so nothing above it on that hop saw a failed model call. The layers stacked here; they did not multiply. It is worth being exact about the reach of that: only one of the two hops in this row carried more than one retrying layer, since R4 puts no stanza on the egress route, so the measured contest is between the gateway and the client on the A2A delivery hop, and the model hop had a single candidate by construction. What this row did **not** test, and should not be read as having tested, is a failure that survives the inner layer's own attempt — the receiver's injection fires once and disarms, so the gateway's retry always succeeded and the client's layer was never reached.

  The composition's masking is itself a measured result rather than a nuisance. A retry configured at the client and a retry configured at the gateway are, from the client's side of the exchange, indistinguishable in this row: one client line, one client span, `http_status` 200, whether the client's own knob was on or off. R2 already measured the gateway alone producing exactly that shape at the client. So the difference between R2 and R4 at the A2A layer is not visible from anywhere the client can see; it is visible only in the model invocation count, which is the layer R3 measured and the one the A2A-level ledgers do not reach. A layer whose retry is masked by an inner one is also a layer whose configuration goes unexercised while it is masked, which is a property of this composition and not a fault in any component of it.

  The classification is **potentially dangerous** on both receivers, and the reason is the row's own counts rather than a counterfactual: two model invocations were made, under one `taskId`, one `messageId` and one delivery that reached dispatch, with a single completed Task returned to a client that wrote one line. This lab's model endpoint is a stateless text completion with nothing to duplicate, but the shape counted here — one Task, one dispatch, two calls to whatever backs the model — is the shape that would double a side effect behind the agent's own model client, and R4 adds a second, independent duplication above it that this particular injection kept from becoming a second Task only because it refuses the first delivery before the SDK sees it. A.1 measured what happens when a byte-identical second delivery does reach dispatch: 2 dispatches, 2 Tasks and 2 model invocations, 20 of 20, at both receivers. So this row's two duplications sit at two different detection depths at once, which no earlier row in this matrix produced: the second delivery is visible at the pre-dispatch ingress ledger, as it was in R1 and R2, and the second model call is visible nowhere above the invocation ledger, as it was in R3, and both happened to the same work item.

  The two receivers agree on every count and differ only in where the evidence sits, which is the same split every earlier Gate 3 row recorded: the Go receiver instruments both deliveries at its own server span and hides its model retry inside one client span; the Python receiver instruments only the delivery that reached its inner app and shows its model retry as two client spans with their own statuses. Neither difference is about what a client or a gateway did to either receiver, and neither changed a count.

- Follow-up: none. Nothing in this row behaved unlike a document read in this session or unlike an earlier measurement in this gate, and nothing looks like a project gap: the gateway's retry, the model clients' retry conditions and the fixtures' injection semantics were all read from source or from earlier counted rows before this row ran, and each fired where those readings said it would. The derivation's single-label output, recorded in Method above, is a property of `experiments/lib/derive-layer.sh` as Task 3 and Task 4 built it and not a defect: both hops' evidence is printed in every `attribution.txt`, and the row's second attribution is that evidence read by rule (c). Task 9's trace-attribution summary should carry both hops for this row rather than the one column `summary.csv` holds.

## Gate 3 / both receivers / egress-route retry — Does an egress gateway retry duplicate a model call, and what does the mock see?
- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.2 openai-python=3.9.0
- Environment: kind
- Method: `make matrix RUN=egress RECEIVER=go REPS=20` and `make matrix RUN=egress RECEIVER=py REPS=20` (`experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`, reused unchanged; this row needed no edit to it or to `experiments/lib/derive-layer.sh`), on 2026-09-09/10, each counted invocation preceded by its own one-repetition dry run under its own nonce whose directory was deleted, twenty repetitions per receiver, forty counted work items in all, RUN_IDs 015255 (go) and 020408 (py), neither reused. **This row is the author's addition and sits outside the proposal's §4.4 A.3 matrix**: it is recorded in `docs/proposal-notes.md` under 2026-09-09, the proposal text is unchanged, and no checklist box belongs to it. Telemetry pins: collector=otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.160.0, jaeger=jaegertracing/jaeger:2.20.0, prometheus=prom/prometheus:v3.14.0, operator=v0.158.0 (Helm chart 0.122.0), otel-go=v1.46.0, otel-go-contrib=v0.71.0, and for the Python agent the OpenTelemetry distro 0.65b0. The certificate check ran first on both invocations and found `VALID CERT true` for `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/lab/sa/default`, so `ztunnel` was not restarted on either; both committed `certificates.txt` files record `NOT AFTER 2026-09-10T19:19:14Z` for that identity.

  **The one layer switched on is the egress route's.** `make retry-on ROUTE=egress` puts `retry: {attempts: 1, backoff: 100ms, codes: [500, 503]}` on `agentgateway-egress/model-via-agw`, the route by which the model host `model.lab.internal` is reached on the `agw-egress` waypoint, under agentgateway's own control plane. `codes` carries 500 as well as 503 because the failure injected on this hop is the model endpoint's own `http500`; both values are inside the set Gateway API v1.6.2 states an implementation must accept as retriable, recorded with its file and line numbers at Task 2 in `experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-pipeline/sources.md` §3. The stanza was read back from the API server rather than from the manifest: 1 on that route and 1 across every HTTPRoute in the cluster, both asserted before anything was sent, and 0 on each of `lab/worker`, `lab/worker-ingress` and `lab/orchestrator-ingress`; the route objects with the stanza on are in `routes.txt` and with it off in `routes-off/routes.txt`. Every other retry layer was asserted off before sending rather than assumed: no `CLIENT_*` variable on any Deployment in `lab`, the loadgen Job rendered `CLIENT_RETRIES=0 CLIENT_SDK_RESEND=off CLIENT_RETRY_ON=transport`, `MODEL_RETRIES` unset on `deployment/worker` and `MODEL_MAX_RETRIES=0` on `deployment/orchestrator`, all read off the live objects. A second model call in this row can therefore only be the egress route's.

  **The injection, and why it stays armed.** The mock is armed per repetition with `POST /control/inject {"mode":"http500","lwi":"<the repetition's work item>"}` after a `POST /control/reset`, and both injectors are reset before and after every repetition. Read from `fixtures/mockllm/injection.go`: `fires(count, lwi)` returns true whenever the call's resolved work item equals the armed `lwi`, with no attempt counter involved, so a work-item-keyed arming stays armed for that work item and answers **every** call carrying it, the re-sent one included. Both the call and its re-send are therefore answered 500, deliberately: this row measures the egress retry's duplication of the model call, not its recovery, which is the same arming and the same reason Task 2's egress mechanics probe used. The mock answers `http500` after its configured ~200 ms latency with the body `{"error":{"message":"injected failure","type":"mockllm_injected"}}`. The receivers' own control endpoints were reset and never armed for this row; the mock's is the only injection on the path.

  **Stimulus and paths**, as in every other matrix row: an in-cluster loadgen Job to the receiver's Service — for the Go receiver that crosses the worker's own istiod-driven agentgateway waypoint, for the Python receiver the card fetch crosses the orchestrator's waypoint and the SendMessage POST enters through the agentgateway ingress the card advertises. The Python receiver ran in model mode: `DOWNSTREAM_A2A_URL` was read off the live Deployment as `http://worker.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080`, unset for the run, confirmed unset on the live object after the rollout, restored and confirmed live again on exit (`knobs.txt`). The harness's image-freshness guard passed before either run and its output is in both `knobs.txt` files: the checkout's Go-sources hash `dc72c724b8308f76baa9f742aa5a7c7086d5d260` equals the `lab.agent-mesh/go-sources` annotation on `deployment/worker` and on `deployment/mockllm`, with running pods `worker=sha256:931e1d24…` and `mockllm=sha256:4a5a227a…`; no step target was run at any point in this row. Counting follows the Gate 2/3 rule: deliveries are the receiver's own arrival-phase ingress lines with `method == "SendMessage"`, dispatched its execution `execute` lines, Tasks the distinct non-empty `taskId` on its execution `state` lines, model invocations the mock's invocation lines excluding `stale-closed`, and the client result loadgen's own client line; `second_delivery_layer` is derived by `experiments/lib/derive-layer.sh` from each repetition's own ledgers and trace, which is handed no knob value. Each invocation's 132 injector control calls all answered 204 (`control.txt`).
- Result: **identical in 20 of 20 on each receiver, and identical between the two receivers on every ledger count**: deliveries **1**, dispatched **1**, distinct `messageId`s **1**, Tasks created **1**, model invocations **2**, client result `task`/`TASK_STATE_FAILED`. The results-table line, per receiver:

  | Retry layer | Deliveries at B (pre-dispatch) | Dispatched by A2A server | Distinct `messageId`s | Tasks created | Model invocations | Classification | Reason |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
  | Egress gateway route (extra row), Go receiver | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | potentially dangerous | a side-effecting model call is made twice by a layer the agent cannot see: one delivery, one Task and one outbound request from the receiver, two calls at the endpoint |
  | Egress gateway route (extra row), Python receiver | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | potentially dangerous | same reason as the Go row; identical counts, and the same single receiver-side request behind two endpoint calls |

  **What the mock saw, checked against every work item's own `invocation.jsonl` rather than only against `summary.csv`**: two lines per work item, 40 of 40 identical on `logical_work_item_id`, on `messageId`, on `taskId` (non-empty, the Task the receiver had already created) and on `caller`, with the **same `body_sha256` on both lines** in 40 of 40, so the model request was replayed byte for byte. Both lines read `injection: http500`, `outcome: http500`. At the receiver's own ingress ledger every arrival carried `A2A-Version: 1.0` and a 294-byte body, and the JSON-RPC response was 200 with a failed Task inside it. **The span shape is the same at both receivers**, and it is what the attribution rests on: exactly **one** `agw-egress POST /*` inbound span per work item, carrying **two** `agw-egress POST mockllm.lab.svc.cluster.local:8080` upstream spans, each parenting one `mockllm POST /v1/chat/completions` server span, with both mock spans carrying the same `lab_message_id`, in 40 of 40. Each receiver made **one** call, one outbound model client span at `http_status` **500** rather than two. **Attribution is `gateway` on the model hop in 40 of 40.**

  **Go receiver.** The Task failed with `model call: status 500` in 20 of 20. The mock's two invocation lines carry `caller: worker` and a per-line latency of 200.05–205.33 ms, which is the mock's own configured latency on each attempt. **10 spans across 2 trace ids** per work item (`agw-egress`=3, `loadgen`=2, `mockllm`=2, `worker`=3), in 20 of 20. The one outbound model client span is `worker HTTP POST`, at `http_status` 500 in 20 of 20, and the receiver's own server span names a parent that no exported span matches, the istiod-driven waypoint, as the baseline measured. Timing: each upstream attempt 200.8–205.8 ms, the gap between the first attempt ending and the second starting 101.3–108.1 ms, the one inbound egress span 504.0–511.2 ms, and the client's own `loadgen HTTP POST` span 505.8–513.9 ms.

  **Python receiver.** The Task failed with `Error code: 500 - {'error': {'message': 'injected failure', 'type': 'mockllm_injected'}}` in 20 of 20, the openai client quoting the mock's own body. The mock's two invocation lines carry `caller: orchestrator` and a per-line latency of 200.19–207.77 ms. **55 spans across 2 trace ids** per work item (`agentgateway-ingress`=2, `agw-egress`=3, `loadgen`=2, `mockllm`=2, `orchestrator`=46), in 20 of 20. The one outbound model client span is `orchestrator POST`, at `http_status` 500 in 20 of 20 — one span rather than two, which is the measurement that separates this row from R3 at this receiver, where openai-python's own retry opened one span per attempt and two calls entered the egress waypoint. Timing: each upstream attempt 200.9–209.1 ms, the gap 101.2–111.4 ms, the one inbound egress span 504.2–516.6 ms, and the `loadgen HTTP POST` span 515.4–527.7 ms.

  **Both receivers.** The gap between the two attempts is the stanza's 100 ms backoff measured from the response rather than from the request, and the whole cost of the duplication reached the caller as latency on a request that failed anyway. The two receivers record the failure in different words but from the same status, unlike the baseline's injected `close`, which reached the two SDKs as a synthesised status at one and as the gateway's own prose at the other; a 500 is a real response and both saw it as one. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-a3-egress-go/` and `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-a3-egress-py/`, each with `summary.csv` (20 rows, the fourteen columns named in `experiments/gate3-matrix.sh`), `knobs.txt`, `control.txt`, `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, `routes.txt`, `routes-off/routes.txt`, and one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json`, `spans.csv` and `attribution.txt`. **In this row `summary.csv`'s `second_delivery_layer` column names the model hop, not a delivery hop**: the column is named for the second delivery every other matrix row measures, and this row has none, so all 40 rows read `deliveries` 1 beside `second_delivery_layer` `gateway` and the `gateway` there is the second model call.
- Interpretation: an egress gateway retry duplicates the model call at both receivers, and the endpoint cannot tell the second call from the first: same work item, same `messageId`, same `taskId`, same caller, same bytes. Every count above the model hop reads as one clean delivery of one message — one arrival, one dispatch, one Task — and the Task's failure says only that the model call failed, not that it was made twice. This is the same 1/1/1/1/2 ledger shape R3 produced, and the difference between the two rows is where the second call was made and therefore who could have counted it. In R3 the receiver's own model client made both attempts: a component the agent owns, configures and could instrument. Here the receiver made exactly one request and got exactly one response, and its own outbound span says so with a single span at `http_status` 500, so **no instrument at or above the receiver, including its own model client, saw the second call**. Below the receiver, two did: the model endpoint's own invocation ledger, and the egress waypoint's own exported spans, which are what this row's `gateway` attribution is derived from. Both sit below the layer where CLAUDE.md rule 5 puts the ledgers this lab builds first, and neither is reachable from the agent's own records. That is a lower detection floor than R3's, which was already lower than R1's and R2's. The classification is **potentially dangerous**: this lab's model endpoint is a stateless text completion with no side effect to duplicate, but the shape measured here — one delivery, one Task, one request from the agent, two calls at whatever backs the model — is exactly the shape that would double a real side effect behind a network policy the agent never sees, and the agent would have no record to reconcile against. Two limits of this row, stated rather than left to be inferred. First, **it says nothing about recovery**: the arming stays armed for the work item, so the second attempt was answered 500 as well, by design, and what an egress retry does when the endpoint's failure is transient is untested at these pins. Second, **it is the one hop R4 left alone** — R4 put no stanza on the egress route — so an egress retry composed with a model-client retry is untested too, and nothing here says how the two would interact. What this row adds to Task 2's egress mechanics probe, which measured the same shape at five repetitions on the Go receiver alone, is twenty repetitions per receiver, the Python receiver's own numbers, the client-visible result and latency, and the receiver-side single-span evidence that the duplication was made below the agent rather than by it.
- Follow-up: none. The stanza's fields and the retriable-code set were read from the pinned Gateway API source at Task 2 and recorded with line numbers there; the mock's arming semantics were read from `fixtures/mockllm/injection.go` in this session; nothing behaved unlike either, and nothing here looks like a project gap in `a2a-go`, `a2a-python`, `openai-python` or agentgateway.

  **What the columns say when read down rather than across.** Deliveries at B is 2 in R1, R2 and R4 and 1 in the baseline, R3 and the egress addition, at both receivers. Dispatched by A2A server and distinct `messageId`s and Tasks created are **1** in every cell of both tables — fourteen filled rows there, plus the two rows of the author's addition below them. Model invocations is 2 in R3, R4 and the egress addition and 1 in the baseline, R1 and R2. So across the whole matrix the pre-dispatch ledger separated the rows that duplicated a delivery, the invocation ledger separated the rows that duplicated a model call, and the execution ledger separated neither: it reads 1 dispatch and 1 Task everywhere.
- Interpretation: the proposal states the classification vocabulary as *"Classification: safe, inefficient, or potentially dangerous for side-effecting operations"* and turns the experiment on *"does transport-layer retry behaviour preserve or violate A2A task lifecycle semantics, and did the implementation exercise the protocol's optional safeguard?"* Answered from the counts above and from A.1's, and from nothing else: in this matrix no transport-layer retry violated the task lifecycle, and none of them preserved it by anything a receiver did. Tasks created is 1 and distinct `messageId`s is 1 in every filled cell of both tables, so no row here produced a second Task — but in R1, R2 and R4 that is because the injection refuses the first delivery before the A2A SDK sees it, leaving the retry as the only delivery that reached dispatch. A.1 counted the other case directly, at both receivers and in 20 of 20 each: a second delivery of the same `messageId` that does reach dispatch is 2 dispatches, 2 Tasks and 2 model invocations, both for M1 (byte-identical, the shape R2's gateway retry and R1's `http` layer put on the wire) and for M2 (same `messageId`, new JSON-RPC id, the shape R1's `sdk` layer puts on the wire). The safeguard the protocol makes optional is duplicate detection keyed on `messageId`, and the counts say plainly that neither implementation exercised it: A.1 recorded 1 distinct `messageId` across both deliveries and 2 Tasks created from them, in 20 of 20, at both receivers, so the identifier a receiver would key on was present on the wire and neither a2a-go v2.5.0 nor a2a-python 1.1.2 used it. That is the whole of the answer at these pins, and it is why every retry row in both tables carries **potentially dangerous** rather than **safe**: the classification is about what the layer can do to a side-effecting call given A.1's measured receiver behaviour, not only about what this matrix's injection point happened to produce.
  
  Three further things the two tables settle that no single row entry does. First, **the two receivers agree on every cell that both tables fill**: each of the proposal's five rows carries the same five numbers at the Python receiver as at the Go one, and so does the author's addition, so nothing in either table distinguishes a2a-go v2.5.0 from a2a-python 1.1.2 by a number. The receivers differ in the error text they record and in where a refused delivery leaves evidence — the baseline entry counted two different failure strings for one injected event, and R1, R2 and R4 all recorded that the Python receiver's pre-dispatch refusal opens no span of its own — and neither difference reached a count. Second, **the rows separate into two detection depths, and the columns show which**. R1 and R2 duplicated a delivery and nothing below it, visible at the pre-dispatch ingress ledger. R3, R4 and the egress addition duplicated a model call, visible only at the invocation ledger, with R4 doing both to the same work item at once. Third, **the same classification label covers three different detection floors**, which is why the reason strings differ where the labels do not: in R3 the receiver's own model client made the second call, a component the agent owns and could instrument; in the egress addition the receiver made exactly one request and only the endpoint's ledger and the egress proxy's own spans recorded the second; and in R1, R2 and R4 the second delivery is countable at the receiver's own first ledger. The proposal allows *"No layer retried under default configuration"* as a valid reportable result, and that is what the baseline row alone found: 40 of 40 single deliveries with no knob set. Every other row switched a named layer on deliberately, and every layer so switched retried, except R4's client layer, which was armed and rendered into every Job and never fired because the gateway below it answered the 503 and returned a 200 upward.
- Follow-up: none. This entry adds no measurement and reports no behaviour of its own; every row it tabulates carries `Follow-up: none` already, and nothing in reading them side by side looks like a project gap.

A.3 R1`, `... A.3 R2`, `... A.3 R3`, `... A.3 R4` and `... egress-route retry` for the per-row evidence. The derivation's rules, as Task 3 built them and Task 4 extended them, and in the order it applies them: **(a)** a second arrival carrying a new JSON-RPC `id` under one `messageId` is `client-sdk`, decided from the ledgers before any span is read; **(b)** a byte-identical second arrival is decided from the two receiver server spans' parentage, in three ordered branches — one shared parent span id is `gateway`, one proxy span having sent the request twice; two distinct parent span ids whose own parents are one shared span of a single service that is neither the client nor the receiver is `gateway` as well, one proxy having made both attempts through two upstream spans of its own; and two distinct parent span ids that do **not** converge on one proxy span is `client-http` (`experiments/lib/derive-layer.sh:327-343`); **(c)** two model invocations under one execution with two inbound egress spans is `model-client`, and with one inbound egress span carrying two upstream attempts is `gateway` on the model hop; **the fallback**, when the receiver recorded fewer server spans than the ledger counted deliveries, reads the nearest proxy that did export a span for the surviving delivery — named from that delivery's own parent span, never assumed — and decides from that proxy's own inbound spans: as many inbound spans as deliveries, each carrying one upstream attempt of its own, is the client layer; one inbound span carrying two upstream attempts is `gateway`; anything else stays `not-attributable`. Never the parent span's service: a proxy sits between the client and the receiver on every path at step 3.   **Where a trace could not attribute a second delivery, and the ledgers still counted it.** Three shapes, all recorded rather than smoothed over.
  1. **The Python receiver's refused delivery opens no span at all**, in every row that injects `http503-before-dispatch` there: R1 both sub-rows, R2 both applicable sub-rows, R4. `IngressMiddleware` is added after `Starlette(routes=routes)` is constructed, so Starlette places it outermost, above the layer the `opentelemetry-instrument` launcher instruments; it answers the refused delivery with a raw ASGI `send()` and returns without calling the inner app. The delivery is on the ingress ledger and seen by the proxy one hop out, and nowhere at the receiver. **80 work items** are attributed through the proxy fallback for this reason (R1 `py/http` 20, R2 `py/ingress` 20 and `py/ingress-incluster` 20, R4 Python 20), and **20 more** (R1 `py/sdk`) are attributed by the ledger rule with no span evidence for the second attempt at all.
  2. **The istiod-driven waypoints never identify themselves.** In every row whose second delivery crossed one — R2 Go `waypoint` 20 work items and R4 Go 20 — the `gateway` label rests on a **shared dangling parent span id** rather than on a span the retrying proxy emitted, because that proxy exports nothing. The attributing evidence is the absence of the span whose id both receiver spans name. Where the two attempts instead carry two distinct dangling parents, that same absence is what rules the gateway out (R1 Go `http`, 20 work items).
  3. **The exported trace is selected by an attribute only a receiver or the mock ever carries.** `make export-trace` queries whole traces by `lab.work_item`, and across R1's 80 work items **0 of 180 `loadgen` spans, 0 of 120 `agentgateway-ingress` spans and 0 of 160 `agw-egress` spans** carry it. A delivery is therefore visible in the export only when its own trace also holds a tagged span, which is why the R1 Python `sdk` sub-row's refused attempt — its own trace id, nothing tagged in it — never comes back, and why the Go `sdk` sub-row's does, its refused attempt having opened a `worker` server span. The fallback's undercount cannot mislabel anything, only fall through: `client-http` needs the exact entry count and `gateway` needs exactly one entry with two upstream attempts. **In all three shapes the ledgers still count**: the pre-dispatch ingress ledger recorded 2 deliveries for every one of the 200, and the invocation ledger recorded 2 calls for every one of the 120, whatever the trace held.

  One historical case belongs here because it is the shape the fallback exists for: R1's Python `http` sub-row **returned `not-attributable` on its first derivation pass**, for exactly the missing-second-receiver-span reason above. The fallback was added and all 120 R1-and-baseline work items were re-derived with it — the 40 baseline and the 60 non-`py/http` R1 work items byte-identical, the 20 `py/http` ones changing to `client-http` — so no `not-attributable` row survives in the committed tree.
- Interpretation: every second delivery and every second model call this matrix produced traces to a layer — 200 second deliveries and 120 second model calls across the six rows, none left unattributed — and the label was decided by the ledgers first and by span structure second in every case, never by which service a parent span belongs to. What the traces added over the ledgers is the layer, and they added it from three different vantage points rather than one: the receiver's own two server spans where the receiver instrumented both deliveries, the proxy in front of it where the receiver instrumented only one, and the egress hop's inbound and upstream counts for everything that happened below the A2A layer. The two receivers needed different vantage points for the same stimulus, and that is a lab wiring fact rather than a difference in what any client or gateway did to either: the Go worker's `otelhttp.Handler` wraps the whole mux, so a delivery refused before dispatch still opens a span, while the Python orchestrator's `IngressMiddleware` sits outside the instrumented app and answers before one is opened. Neither difference reached a count. The one hop that stayed dark at these pins is the istiod-driven agentgateway waypoint: it appears in no work item's spans-by-service list anywhere in the matrix, and it is the hop that did the retrying in 40 of them; that its own span never appears is what Task 1 measured and what every waypoint row here attributes around, by treating the dangling parent as the evidence it is. Ledgers are ground truth and traces are the explanation, which is the division `docs/PROPOSAL.md` §4.3 sets out, and this matrix is a case where the explanation was available for every count without the ledgers ever needing it to be.
- Follow-up: none. The two open drafts the trace work produced are already recorded against the entry that measured them — `docs/upstream/otel-operator-python-injection-shadows-app-dependencies.md` and `docs/upstream/agentgateway-policy-attached-to-istiod-driven-waypoint.md`, both drafts, neither filed — and nothing in reading the six rows' attributions side by side is a new project gap. The waypoint's own silence is recorded there as not documented rather than as a contradiction, and it stays that way here.

Telemetry pins: collector=otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.160.0, jaeger=jaegertracing/jaeger:2.20.0, prometheus=prom/prometheus:v3.14.0, otel-go=v1.46.0, otel-go-contrib=v0.71.0, and for the Python agent the OpenTelemetry distro 0.65b0 with exporter 1.44.0 and the Starlette and httpx instrumentations at 0.65b0 — the same list the trace-per-work-item entry names, less the operator, which no longer exists on the cluster, and less the Python auto-instrumentation image, which no pod on this cluster ever ran. Spans, worker receiver: **8 spans** across **2 trace ids**, by service `loadgen`=2, `worker`=3, `agw-egress`=2, `mockllm`=1; `lab.work_item` on **3 of 8**. Orchestrator receiver: **62 spans** across **2 trace ids**, by service `loadgen`=2, `agentgateway-ingress`=2, `orchestrator`=53, `worker`=2, `agw-egress`=2, `mockllm`=1; `lab.work_item` on **5 of 62**. Hops that produced no span: the istiod-driven agentgateway waypoints and only those — `agentgateway-waypoint` for the worker receiver, both it and `agentgateway-waypoint-orch` for the orchestrator receiver — and each work item carries exactly **2 spans whose parent span id names no exported span**, the same dangling-parent count the committed entry measured. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-a3-operator-removed/` (`summary.csv`, one directory per work item holding the three ledgers, `client.jsonl`, `trace.json` and `spans.csv`, plus `certificates.txt`, `cluster-versions.txt`, `operator-removal.txt`, `operator-deletion.txt` and `post-run-cluster.txt`).

The one thing worth naming for anyone repeating the deletion is that `helm uninstall` removed the four CRDs, which is not what the ordered commands assumed — the explicit CRD deletion answered `NotFound` four times — and that deleting the CRD is what removed the `lab-python` Instrumentation, since a custom resource cannot outlive its API. ## Gate 3 / both receivers / images rebuilt — Do the counts and the trace shape survive the image rebuild (latest Go, python:3.14, Debian 13 distroless, read-only root filesystems, non-root, no ServiceAccount token)?

Observed here — `python:3.14-slim` → `sha256:cad9a2c871761c413caa6fdd6441c783451e740a48aaeba60ae62a8b53525ef6`, **CPython 3.14.7**; `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest` → `sha256:73d2665b478d8fa2de1cf105c6841f8e9cb6b09e568fc7700440c09f8fcd7ac4`, builder printing **uv 0.12.12**; `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot` → `sha256:1c2c046bc09ed40fad370b599a0b1ae7987f55b01e247cf27a7c27cd97e5bbc7`, config `User=65532`, from ko's own "Using base" line for both Go binaries. The final stage of the Python image upgrades the OS in one layer before the user is created; on this date it applied nothing — "0 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 0 to remove and 0 not upgraded" against fetched `trixie-updates` and `trixie-security` indexes — the base already carrying trixie's current patch level. Application files in that image are **root-owned**, no `--chown`, so the process cannot rewrite its own code or dependencies. Ledgers per work item: worker receiver 2 ingress lines, 1 `received`, 1 `execute`, 1 Task through `SUBMITTED`→`WORKING`→`COMPLETED`, 1 invocation; orchestrator receiver 4 ingress lines, 2 `received`, 2 `execute` and 2 Tasks, one at each agent on the forward path, 1 invocation, which is the worker's. Hops that produced no span: the istiod-driven agentgateway waypoints and only those, and exactly **2 dangling parents per work item**. No ingress line carries a `truncated` field. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-images-rebuilt/`. An earlier rollout of this branch, before the author's second-round decisions, produced a run of its own; it is kept rather than discarded, under `pre-redo/` and `clean-check/pre-redo/` with a README in each, beside the versions of `image-after.txt`, `image-size.txt`, `readonly-proofs.txt`, `readonly-run.txt` and `cluster-rollout.txt` that describe those first images. **It produced the same figures** — 8 and 62 spans over 2 trace ids, 3-of-8 and 5-of-62, and 1/1/1/1/1 on the clean check — on images with digest-pinned bases, a venv owned by 65532, no OS-upgrade layer, the Go binaries on distroless Debian 12 and the ServiceAccount token still mounted. The entry cites the top-level run; the pre-redo one is the record that none of those differences moved a count either.

Four things changed at once under the agents — a different build system for the Python image, a different base and interpreter (3.13 → 3.14.7), a different Debian for the Go images (12 → 13), a different architecture (emulated amd64 → native arm64) — alongside a read-only root filesystem, a dropped capability set, root-owned application files and no ServiceAccount token on every workload, and **not one count moved**. The same 8 and 62 spans over the same two trace ids, the same per-service split, the same 3-of-8 and 5-of-62 attribute coverage, the same two dark waypoint hops, the same two dangling parents, and 1/1/1 with a completed Task at each agent. That is the useful result: what the earlier Gate 3 entries measured is a property of the mesh and the SDKs at these pins, not of how either image happened to be assembled, which Debian it sat on, or which architecture it was emulating. The hardening cost nothing at all — no container needed an `emptyDir` and none noticed the missing token, on the first attempt, which the code grep had predicted and the host run had already shown — and it is worth saying why: every instrument in this lab writes JSON to stdout and nothing in it talks to the Kubernetes API, so the ledgers are the reason there was nothing to write and the design is the reason there was no token to read. Three things are recorded rather than smoothed over. The size comparison points in two directions depending on which command asks, and the filesystem measurement is the one that answers the question actually asked; the two-thirds reduction the `.Size` field appears to show is mostly gzip. The OS-upgrade layer applied nothing on this date, which is the counted answer and not a disappointment — the base tag was already current, and the layer earns its place the day it is not. And with `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` and `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` unset, `opentelemetry-instrument` prints a configurator failure, the `otlp` entry point for those two signals belonging to the meta package while this project pins `opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http` only — a property of the pinned dependency set that the buildpack image shared, invisible here because `deploy/step-3-stress` has always set all three exporter variables. Letting three base images float to their tags changed no digest on this date: every one resolved to what a digest pin would have named, which is a fact of 2026-09-10 and not a property of the arrangement.
- Follow-up: none.

## Gate 3 / n/a / image vulnerability scan — What does Kubescape count in each of our images on this date?
- Versions: k8s=v1.37.0@sha256:a1ed56cfb0e7b93589bdf97c8cd566405a265939e3620fc4f5de89adff580ae5 istio=1.31.0 agentgateway=v1.5.0 gateway-api=v1.6.2, experimental a2a-spec=3303592588e388e62e0f69f701af531d2f4e3991 a2a-go=v2.5.0 a2a-python=1.1.2 openai-python=3.9.0
- Environment: kind
- Method: `make scan-images` on 2026-09-10, over the five images this lab builds — the Python agent (`orchestrator:dev`, two stages on `python:3.14-slim`, CPython 3.14.7) and the four Go binaries (worker, mockllm, loadgen, replay, all on `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot`). Scanner: **Kubescape 4.0.14**, build commit `031cd40cc8de696fa30a648001853443019ec97a`, build date 2026-09-09T12:24:41Z, installed with `brew install kubescape` — the route `https://kubescape.io/docs/install-cli/` gives for macOS — and matching the v4.0.14 that `releases/latest` named the same day. Chosen because Kubescape is a **CNCF incubating project** (`https://www.cncf.io/projects/`, read this session) and Trivy and Grype are not. Command per image, as `https://kubescape.io/docs/scanning/` documents it: `kubescape scan image <image:tag> --format json --output <name>.json`. **Vulnerability database built 2026-09-10**, as every scan reported; the counts belong to that database date as much as to the scanner version. This is a **host-side CLI only**: nothing was installed in the cluster — no Kubescape Operator, no node agent, no host scanner, no CRD, no namespace — so the cluster's component list is exactly what `CLAUDE.md` rule 6 allows. The scope widening is the author's decision of 2026-09-10, recorded in `docs/proposal-notes.md`. Kubescape reads the local Docker daemon rather than the kind node's containerd store, so the four Go images were rebuilt for the scan with `KO_DOCKER_REPO=ko.local ko build ./agents/worker ./fixtures/mockllm ./fixtures/loadgen ./fixtures/replay --platform=linux/arm64`, from the same checkout, the same `.ko.yaml` base tag and the same toolchain the rollout used; ko's log for that build reads `Using base gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot@sha256:1c2c046bc09ed40fad370b599a0b1ae7987f55b01e247cf27a7c27cd97e5bbc7`, the same index digest the `make step-3` build resolved.
- Result: **175 matches across the five images, and 170 of them are in one image.** (corrected 2026-09-10; the text read 173) By image, from `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-images-rebuilt/scan/summary.csv`, as `total (critical/high/medium/low/negligible/unknown)`: **orchestrator 170 (7/58/46/7/44/8)**; **loadgen 3 (0/3/0/0/0/0)**; **worker 1 (0/1/0/0/0/0)**; **mockllm 1 (0/1/0/0/0/0)**; **replay 0**. The four Go images carry 5 matches between them and no Critical at all; the Python image carries 170 including all 7 Criticals. The components Kubescape named most often in the Python image are the Debian base's own: `perl-base` (5 Critical, 7 High, 4 Medium, 1 Negligible), `libc-bin` and `libc6` (1 Critical, 2 High, 3 Medium, 1 Low, 7 Negligible, 4 Unknown each), `bsdutils` and `libblkid1` (4 High, 1 Medium, 1 Negligible each). Provenance, recorded in `scan-context.txt` rather than assumed: the four ko image IDs scanned do **not** equal the ones the lab pods run, because ko rebuilds unchanged sources to a new digest on every apply — a property this repository measured earlier (`experiments/runs/2026-09-09-a3-pipeline/replicasets.txt`) — so what is equal is the input, not the artefact: same Go-sources hash `dc72c724b8308f76baa9f742aa5a7c7086d5d260` (the value stamped on both Deployments), same base index digest, same toolchain. The orchestrator's two identifiers differ for an unrelated reason and **are** the same build: the daemon holds `sha256:9d30a65a...210668f8` and the pod reports `import-2026-09-10@sha256:f811f975...aabe16c4`, which is `kind load docker-image` re-importing into the node's containerd store and computing its own digest — the rollout log shows that load carrying the daemon ID scanned here. Every counted finding is in the tree per image as `<image>-findings.csv`, columns `id,severity,package,version,fixed_in,type`, sorted by severity then id; **the row count of each equals that image's `total` in `summary.csv` and their per-severity counts equal its columns** — 170, 3, 1, 1 and 0 respectively, checked for all five. Run outputs: `experiments/runs/2026-09-10-images-rebuilt/scan/` (the five per-image CSVs, one text report per image, four of the five JSON reports, `summary.csv`, `scan-context.txt`, `ko-build.txt`). `orchestrator.json` is not committed: Kubescape wrote it at **757325 bytes**, which is not the small CSV or JSONL `CLAUDE.md` asks for, and `make scan-images` regenerates it; the CSV derived from it carries every one of its 170 findings, and the derivation is `experiments/lib/kubescape-findings.jq`, which `make scan-images` itself runs — the same program reproduces the four committed small images' CSVs byte-for-byte.
- Interpretation: what was found, stated plainly and left alone. **166 of the orchestrator's 170 findings have an empty `fixed_in`** — no fix available — and that includes **all 7 Criticals and all 58 Highs**; Medium is 43 of 46, Low 6 of 7, Negligible 44 of 44, Unknown 8 of 8. The four that do carry a fix are CPython itself, `python` 3.14.7, and every one of them names a 3.15 pre-release as the fix: CVE-2025-15367 → 3.15.0a6, CVE-2026-15806 and CVE-2026-17084 → 3.15.0rc2 (all Medium), CVE-2026-15310 → 3.15.0rc2 (Low). So there is nothing on this image that an upgrade at these pins would remove, which is the same fact the `apt-get upgrade` layer reported from the other side when it found nothing to apply: the archive has no newer package to offer. The four Go images are the opposite case — **every one of their 5 findings has a fix**, and all five are Go modules rather than operating-system packages: `google.golang.org/grpc` v1.83.1 → 1.83.2 (GHSA-2v4p-qf9q-27wj, High) in worker, mockllm and loadgen, and `golang.org/x/mod` v0.38.0 → 0.40.0 (GO-2026-6179 and GO-2026-6180, both High) in loadgen alone. `replay` has none because it imports neither. Both are indirect dependencies in `go.mod`. The gap between 170 and 5 is the base image, not the code: the Go binaries sit on a distroless static image that ships almost no userland, so there is next to nothing for a package scanner to match, while the Python agent needs an interpreter and therefore a Debian userland, and every package in that userland is in scope for the scanner whether the agent calls it or not. `perl-base`, which carries 5 of the 7 Criticals, is one the agent never invokes. That is a statement about what a package-level scan counts, not a judgement about exposure: this scan matches installed package versions against a database, it does not ask whether a path is reachable from the agent's code, and nothing here should be read as saying the Python image is thirty-four times more exposed than the Go ones. Two things bound the number further. The final stage of the Python image already runs an `apt-get upgrade` before the user is created, and on this date it had nothing to apply — `python:3.14-slim` was at Debian 13 trixie's current patch level — so these 170 are not a lag behind the archive; they are what the archive itself has open at this database date. And the count is a function of the database, built 2026-09-10, as much as of the image: the same five images scanned next week give other numbers, which is why the database date is recorded beside the scanner version. **Nothing was changed in response to any of this** — no base moved, no dependency re-pinned, no package held — because a fix is the author's decision and because a scan that changed the images would make every other count in this file describe images that no longer exist.
- Follow-up: none.

What did **not** move is equally counted. The orchestrator's 170 findings are the same 170, byte for byte in the CSV, because nothing about that image changed — its Python sources, its lockfile and its base were untouched and the image itself was not rebuilt. The previous entry recorded why they stay: 166 of the 170 carry an empty `fixed_in`, including all 7 Criticals and all 58 Highs, so there is no version to move to at these pins, and the four that do carry one name a CPython 3.15 pre-release.
